name: dsh-acp
catalogDescription: Automation-only Agent Client Protocol server for driving DeepSeek Harness agents over JSON-RPC stdio
manifestDescription: Automation-only Agent Client Protocol server for driving DeepSeek Harness agents over JSON-RPC stdio

readme.description: Automation-only ACP (Agent Client Protocol) server for programmatic clients and maintainers driving DeepSeek Harness agents over JSON-RPC stdio.
readme.summary: `dsh-acp` lets trusted programs automate persistent DeepSeek Harness agents through the standard [ACP](https://agentclientprotocol.com): create or resume sessions, select a model and reasoning effort, attach MCP servers, submit or cancel work, receive semantic updates, and close sessions independently. Choose it for out-of-process subagents, test runners, and scripted controllers; it intentionally omits DSH-specific presentation data and interactive UI features. Persistence supports listing, resuming, and closing sessions across process restarts, but deletion, forks, transcript replay, and additional directories are unsupported. Run `pnpm dsh --profile acp` to start the server; use `dsh-subagent-acp` as the repository client.

plain.headline: Let other programs drive the assistant
plain.oneLiner: Turns the harness into a service other programs can drive, with no chat window.
plain.whatItDoes: Runs the harness as a background service that trusted programs can connect to. Those programs can start or resume sessions, pick a model, attach extra tools, submit work, cancel it, and read progress updates.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how a script or a test runner can use the assistant without a person sitting in the chat window.
useWhen: You are writing a script or test runner that needs the assistant.
You want an assistant running in its own separate process.
You need sessions that can be resumed after a restart.
skipWhen: You only ever use the assistant through the normal chat window.
You need the on-screen cards, plans, or terminal views.
pros: Trusted programs can create, resume and close sessions.
A program can choose the model and how much reasoning effort to use.
Work can be submitted or cancelled on request.
Sessions can be listed and resumed after a restart.
cons: Only one main workspace is supported; extra folders are not.
Session deletion, forks and replaying an old transcript are not supported.
It leaves out the screens, cards and other interactive parts of the normal app.
Only PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF images can be sent in a prompt.
Connected tool servers can offer tools, but not their resources or prompts.

name: dsh-acp-app
catalogDescription: The dsh ACP profile bundle: automation-only JSON-RPC stdio and process lifecycle over dsh-base
manifestDescription: The dsh ACP profile bundle: automation-only JSON-RPC stdio and process lifecycle over dsh-base

readme.description: Automation-only ACP stdio application profile for users and maintainers launching persistent harness agents.
readme.summary: The automation-only ACP stdio application as a `dsh` profile bundle over [`dsh-base`](../base/README.md). It inherits the base's disabled module-HMR policy; its patch sets the coding-agent persona and default model route, mounts an app-owned zero-option command provider, and starts [`dsh-acp`](../../acp/acp/README.md) only after that provider accepts the invocation. `dsh --profile acp --help` therefore writes help and exits without claiming stdin or stdout.

plain.headline: A ready-made setup for that service
plain.oneLiner: Add-on pack that starts the automation-only service with sensible defaults.
plain.whatItDoes: An add-on pack that starts the whole automation-only service in one step. It also sets the assistant's instructions and default model, and keeps the connection free for traffic between the two programs.
plain.whyYoudCare: You would only want this if you plan to launch the automation service yourself instead of assembling its parts.
useWhen: You want to start the automation service with a single launch command.
You are building your own launch setup for automation work.
skipWhen: You use the assistant through the normal app.
You are not launching any automation yourself.
pros: One launch command starts the whole automation service.
It reserves the connection for traffic between the two programs only.
It shuts down cleanly when the client disconnects or you press Ctrl+C.
New sessions still get a title, without asking the model to invent one.
cons: Changing its settings needs a restart, because live reloading is switched off.
If you build your own launch setup you must keep this part, or nothing will answer the client.
Another add-on that prints to the console can break the connection.

name: dsh-agent
catalogDescription: Agent interface, registry, initiator scope, and event vocabulary for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Agent interface, registry, initiator scope, and event vocabulary for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The Agent handle, live registry, process-local initiator scope, and agent/* event vocabulary for plugins, UI, and orchestrators building or extending agents.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-agent` to create or resume live agents, send follow-up or steering input, inject model-facing context, cancel work, and wait for idle completion. Plugins, UI, hooks, and orchestrators can also observe or intercept agent activity and apply capabilities to one agent without affecting others. Choose it when code needs to control or extend live agents through the public `Agent` API. Pair it with an agent driver such as `dsh-agent-loop`; this package does not create model requests by itself. Initiator attribution is process-local and must be carried explicitly across workers, processes, durable queues, and restarts.

headings.text: Intercept or observe work in flight

plain.headline: Manages every running assistant
plain.oneLiner: The shared control point for starting, steering and stopping running assistants.
plain.whatItDoes: Keeps track of the live assistants in a session. Other parts use it to start or resume an assistant, send more input, add context, cancel work, and wait for it to go idle.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the shared handle that every other part uses to talk to a running assistant, so it needs nothing from you.
useWhen: You are writing code that controls or extends a running assistant.
You want to watch what an assistant is doing, or step in.
skipWhen: You only chat with the assistant and never write add-ons.
pros: You can start, resume, steer and cancel assistants through one consistent interface.
Several assistants can run side by side without interfering with each other.
Other parts can watch an assistant's activity and act on it.
cons: Who started a piece of work is only known inside the current process, so it must be carried across by hand.
Cancelling throws away queued and follow-up work unless you ask to keep it.
There is no way to stop just one step and let the rest of the turn continue.
A message merged from several sources can only name one of them.
It does nothing on its own and needs a driver before any model is called.

name: dsh-agent-instructions
catalogDescription: Workspace context loader for AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md instruction files
manifestDescription: Workspace context loader for AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md instruction files

readme.description: Workspace-instruction context for users and maintainers enabling, sizing, or debugging AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md loading and refresh.
readme.summary: `dsh-agent-instructions` gives agents workspace guidance from user-global and project-level `AGENTS.md`-compatible files. It loads the applicable chain for the first request. It does not watch external edits continuously: successful filesystem operations discover newly relevant nested files and make later changes or removals visible, while session resume reconciles the baseline. `dsh-base` enables this behavior by default, while profiles can disable it. A byte budget bounds the injected context: broader files are omitted before the most specific file is truncated, and an empty chain adds nothing.

plain.headline: Read your project's own rule files
plain.oneLiner: Loads the AGENTS.md-style guidance stored in your project into each session.
plain.whatItDoes: Reads the guidance files you keep in a project, such as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and their local variants, and gives them to the assistant at the start of a session.
plain.whyYoudCare: Your written house rules reach the assistant automatically instead of you retyping them into every conversation.
useWhen: You keep a file of project rules or conventions.
You want the same guidance applied in every session on that project.
skipWhen: You have no such files, so there is nothing to read.
You would rather state your instructions in each conversation.
pros: Project rules load by themselves at the first request.
A size limit keeps the guidance from crowding out your actual work.
Local overlay files can add notes for one machine.
cons: Only its own file tools trigger a refresh, so changes made in a shell are not noticed.
There is no continuous watching; edits appear at the next successful file operation, or when a session resumes.
Lower-case file names, .claude/rules/ folders and @path imports are not understood.
A linked shortcut instruction file is followed, so a cloned project can pull in text from outside its folder.

name: dsh-agent-loop
catalogDescription: The concrete agent loop plugin for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: The concrete agent loop plugin for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The default agent driver for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging how agents are created and how turns and steps run.
readme.summary: `dsh-agent-loop` creates fresh agents or resumes persisted sessions, then drives each turn through model requests, streamed responses, tool execution, and durable session history. Mount it for standard agent compositions; declarative entries start agents at boot, while the public `ctx.agents` API supports programmatic creation and resume. `maxParallelToolCalls` limits concurrent parallel-safe calls, and exclusive calls retain ordering. Cancellation preserves streamed text already delivered to the user. Choose a custom `Agent` implementation only when the standard "call model, run tools, repeat" lifecycle is insufficient.

rationale:
Agents created at startup. The base stays empty; raw overlays may create
agents, while Web creates sessions on client request.

plain.headline: The engine that runs each turn
plain.oneLiner: The core engine that turns your message into model calls, tool runs and saved history.
plain.whatItDoes: Drives a turn from start to finish: it asks the model, streams the answer back, runs the tools the model asks for, and saves the history. It can also pick up a saved session where it left off.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the part that actually does the work when you send a message, so it needs no setting from you.
useWhen: You want assistants that call the model, run tools, and repeat.
You want sessions listed in a setup file to start at launch.
skipWhen: You are replacing the whole assistant engine with one of your own.
pros: Model requests, streamed answers, tool runs and saved history are handled in one place.
Several tool calls can run at once while order-sensitive ones stay exclusive.
Text already shown to you survives a cancellation.
cons: It has no built-in limit on how long a turn runs; stopping a runaway turn takes another part cancelling it.
Sessions started from a setup file get a fresh name on every launch unless you give a stable one.
Assistants defined in a setup file cannot have their own persona or their own set of tools.
Calls whose safety depends on comparing other calls must be marked exclusive.
Recovery from a failed step does not rewrite unanswered calls in turns that already closed.

plain.headline: Write down a set of abilities
plain.oneLiner: Writes down named sets of abilities that a session can choose from.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets you describe a named set of abilities, meaning which tools, prompt text and skills an assistant gets, in an ordinary settings file. You can define several and let a session choose one.
plain.whyYoudCare: These named sets are what you choose between when a session picks which kind of assistant to use.
useWhen: You want a session to have only some tools rather than everything.
You want several ready-made kinds of assistant to choose between.

catalogDescription: Agent-plane presentation selector: composes one agent's tools as PTC mode, native, or both
manifestDescription: Agent-plane presentation selector: composes one agent's tools as PTC mode, native, or both

readme.description: The agent-plane presentation selector for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging which form of its tools an agent preset's models see.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-agent-tool-presentation` in an [agent preset](../../preset/agent-preset-registry/README.md) to fix whether models see every native tool schema, only `run_code` with a generated SDK, or both forms. Each preset can choose independently, so native and PTC agents can share one process without sharing tool catalogs. Selecting `ptc` or `both` requires a compatible PTC runtime; a deployment without one rejects the preset at mount time before its first prompt. The `mode` field is required when this package is present, while omitting the package keeps the deployment default.

plain.whyYoudCare: It changes what the assistant may call directly, so it matters only if you build your own assistant setups.

You want one program to offer both styles to different sessions.
skipWhen: You use the setups that ship with the app.
You do not care how tools are presented to the model.

Two sessions in one program can use different styles at the same time.
Leaving it out keeps the program-wide default.
cons: Choosing the code-running style needs a matching runtime; without one, the setup is rejected when it loads.
It cannot supply that runtime itself, because the host program has to provide it.
The mode setting is required whenever this package is present.

name: dsh-anonymous-user-id
catalogDescription: Shared anonymous user identity for DeepSeek Harness telemetry and feedback correlation
manifestDescription: Shared anonymous user identity for DeepSeek Harness telemetry and feedback correlation

readme.description: Anonymous per-harness-home identity for users and maintainers tracing how telemetry, feedback acknowledgement, and DeepSeek provider requests correlate records.
readme.summary: DeepSeek Harness uses one anonymous identifier per harness home to correlate telemetry, feedback, and DeepSeek requests from the same installation without identifying the user. The random UUID is stored in `$DSH_HOME/.anonymous-user-id` (`$DSH_HOME` defaults to `~/.dsh`), persists across restarts, and is regenerated after you delete the file. Different harness homes use different identifiers, and the value contains no machine or account data. Built-in features create and attach it automatically; package consumers can reuse the same value for installation-scoped correlation, but cannot join records across homes.

Using it in your own package

plain.headline: One anonymous id per installation
plain.oneLiner: Internal anonymous id for the installation. Nothing for you to configure.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that gives your installation one anonymous identifier, which ties telemetry, feedback, and requests together. Features use it automatically, so nothing needs configuring.

cons: If the program exits, a sign-in that was in progress cannot be resumed from the screen.
Your credentials and request tokens are not available through these commands.

name: dsh-api-gateway
catalogDescription: Typert Remote Host dispatcher and Client API endpoint
manifestDescription: Typert Remote Host dispatcher and Client API endpoint

readme.description: Typed Client-to-Host calls and streams: dispatch, validation, cancellation, reconnection, and forwarded Host events.
readme.summary: Two-sided Typert RPC endpoint for Host and Client Cordis environments. The Host entry provides `ctx.typertGateway`, while `@deepseek-ai/dsh-api-gateway/client` provides `ctx.remote`; both consume the same generated `InvocationDescriptor` contract and leave business selection to API Remotes. Connection carries unary request correlation, trust, and response envelopes, while Gateway owns multiplexed Remote streams, each carrying a Client-to-Host uplink on the same logical stream.

plain.headline: Carries requests from the page to the app
plain.oneLiner: The link that carries requests between the web page and the program on your machine.
plain.whatItDoes: It is the connection that carries every request between the web page you click in and the program running on your machine, so the page can ask for things and get answers back.

You are a developer wiring a new screen into the web interface.
skipWhen: You use the harness through its normal web interface, where this is already running.

Carries many live streams over a single connection.
Both sides follow one agreed set of messages instead of guessing.
cons: When a request fails, the page may get an empty explanation instead of the real cause.
Messages sent while the page is disconnected are not replayed afterwards.
Error causes survive only when both sides run in the same process.
Message shapes are checked for valid data, not for whether they suit the task.
Forwarded updates are not filtered or trimmed before they cross.

readme.summary: Use `dsh-atomic-write` to replace a file without exposing partial content or following a symlinked temporary path. plain.whatItDoes: Carries every call between the page in your browser and the app that serves it: sign-in state, reconnecting after a drop, and responses that include file data.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what makes the browser page work, and it sets how large a request can be and how long a sign-in lasts.
useWhen: You open the app in a browser rather than the desktop app.
You need to know how large an upload the page accepts, or how to sign everyone out.
skipWhen: You only ever use the desktop app.
You only reach the page through this machine's own loopback address and nothing else.
pros: The page reconnects after a drop and offers one command to retry at once
A handler can return file bytes alongside a reply, not just plain text
There is a stated size cap, chosen so ordinary images and requests still fit
cons: Buffered web routes hold each whole request in memory, up to a default cap of 300 MiB
The browser sign-in cookie is not marked secure, so plaintext networking can expose it
There is no sign-out: clearing the cookie ends one session, and revoking all needs more

name: dsh-client-file-upload
catalogDescription: Agent-scoped browser file upload, streaming intake, and staged receipt service
manifestDescription: Agent-scoped browser file upload, streaming intake, and staged receipt service

readme.description: Session-addressed browser file uploads with streaming intake, progress, cancellation, and staged receipts for later prompts.
readme.summary: This package lets browser features store a `Blob`, exact bytes, or a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` for one Session and receive an opaque receipt for a later prompt. Served pages send Blob and stream bodies without aggregating their bytes on the page thread; pages whose Host runs in another execution context supply a Fetch-shaped carrier before Cordis boots. Callers can observe consumed bytes and cancel an active operation. A stream body is consumed once and transfers ownership when it crosses a Worker boundary. Exact bytes use the generated Remote.

rationale:
Raw Blob and ReadableStream uploads run independently of Connection's
RPC and generation service.

plain.headline: Hand files from the page to a session
plain.oneLiner: Moves files you pick in the browser into a session, with progress and cancel.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets a page in your browser hand a file, exact bytes, or a stream to one session and get a receipt it can use in a later prompt.
plain.whyYoudCare: It moves a file you pick in the browser into the session that will work on it, without gathering the whole file on the page first.
useWhen: You attach a file in the browser page.
You want to watch upload progress or cancel an upload in progress.
skipWhen: You expect to resume an upload after a failure; retries start from the first byte.
You need a total for a streamed upload; only consumed bytes are reported.
pros: You get upload progress, including the total when the browser knows it
You can cancel an upload while it is running
A streamed file is sent as it is read instead of being held on the page
It also works when the page and the app run in different places, given a small carrier
cons: Uploads cannot be resumed; a failed or cancelled retry starts from the first byte
A stream can be sent only once, so a retry needs a freshly created stream
Progress on a streamed upload shows bytes sent but never a total
The upload helper inside the browser cannot pull in extra code without a separate build

name: dsh-client-hmr
catalogDescription: Web client graph synchronization and rebuilt-bundle reload transport
manifestDescription: Web client graph synchronization and rebuilt-bundle reload transport

readme.description: Live graph synchronization and development bundle reloads for Web client plugins.
readme.summary: `dsh-client-hmr` keeps open Web pages in sync with the Host plugin graph and reloads rebuilt browser bundles. Ordinary plugin enable/disable changes take effect without reloading the page or restarting the Host. Code rebuilds replace the affected plugin with fresh component state. The model sees no new input or output.

rationale:
The client-plugin reload chain, always mounted: it is idle until a
rebuild watcher (pnpm run dev:web) actually rewrites client bundles. It
is a row rather than a child of web-runtime because its node half is a
client-side package, which a host-side bundle cannot import.

plain.headline: Update open pages without a refresh
plain.oneLiner: Applies plugin changes to open pages right away, with no refresh.
plain.whatItDoes: Keeps open pages in step with plugin changes, so switching a plugin on or off takes effect with no refresh and no restart. Built page code can also be swapped in as it is rebuilt.
plain.whyYoudCare: Mostly it is for people building plugins, but it is why a change can reach an open page without a restart.
useWhen: You are building a plugin and want changes to appear without refreshing.
You switch a plugin on or off and want it to apply immediately.
skipWhen: You need a failed rebuild to roll back to the previous version; it does not.
You care about keeping the on-screen state of the plugin being reloaded.
pros: Plugin on and off changes apply without a page refresh or a restart
A rebuilt plugin is replaced while the rest of the page keeps running
It shows the assistant nothing new, so it does not change replies
cons: A reload discards the on-screen state inside that plugin; shared data is kept
There is no rollback: if the replacement fails, the previous code is not restored
It serves the web page only, not the desktop installation or a backend restart

Your choice is remembered on this machine for pages served locally
A new browser starts in the first language that browser asks for
Plugin authors can add their own translated text to the same list

name: dsh-client-modules
catalogDescription: Client module system, dual-face: node half composes the __DSH_BOOT__ entry graph (incremental dsh.client scan, bundle route, index tap, webPlugins service); browser half is the lazy-CJS module table the vendored cordis Loader consumes as its internal seam
manifestDescription: Client module system, dual-face: node half composes the __DSH_BOOT__ entry graph (incremental dsh.client scan, bundle route, index tap, webPlugins service); browser half is the lazy-CJS module table the vendored cordis Loader consumes as its internal seam

readme.description: Client module system for the web GUI: the host composes the boot graph and serves plugin bundles, and the browser loads them lazily, for users and maintainers composing or debugging client plugins.
readme.summary: `dsh-client-modules` turns a plugin package's `dsh.client` declaration into a loadable browser bundle: the host half scans enabled Loader entries and composes the boot graph, an available Web carrier serves each bundle over `/plugins`, and a shell-owned carrier dispatches the same exact bundle responses through `fetchBundle()`. The browser half loads those bundles lazily on demand. Plugin bundles execute lazily — running a bundle only registers a factory, and module side effects run at materialization — so nothing runs until a plugin is first used. Everything here is browser-kernel machinery; the model never sees it.

rationale:
── browser plugin roster (dsh.client rows; node halves are layer-2 hosts) ──
Dual-face: the node half scans this tree, composes window.__DSH_BOOT__,
and serves /plugins/<id>/client.js; the browser half is the module table
the shell kernel constructs before cordis exists (adopted as a plugin
entry by the kernel, never fetched).

plain.headline: Load plugin code into the page
plain.oneLiner: Loads browser plugin code on demand; nothing the assistant can see.
plain.whatItDoes: Turns an add-on package's browser declaration into code the page can load on demand. Plugin code runs only when it is first used, and the assistant never sees any of it.
plain.whyYoudCare: Only if you build browser plugins: it saves wiring each one into the page by hand.
useWhen: You are building a plugin that draws part of the web interface.
You want to understand why a plugin's browser code loads late.
skipWhen: You only use plugins other people wrote.
pros: A plugin declares itself once and the page wiring is automatic
Plugin code is not loaded until it is first needed
It is already running with the web interface, so there is nothing to switch on
cons: It tracks file metadata, not content, so a metadata-only change can reload a plugin
A change invisible in time or size cannot be told apart from no change
Every loaded plugin is one flat unit, so you cannot fetch only part of it
Requested bodies stay cached, and an old debug map request can read the current file

name: dsh-client-product-analytics

manifestDescription: Desktop product event collection and authenticated Host reporting

readme.description: Configure Desktop product analytics, identity fields, and event timing without collecting Web usage.

plain.headline: Report how the desktop app is used
plain.oneLiner: Reports desktop app usage events by default, with no switch in the interface.
plain.whatItDoes: In the desktop app, a chosen set of interactions is sent to the product's own data exporter by default. Pages opened in a browser do not send these events.
plain.whyYoudCare: It decides whether using the desktop app sends usage events, and the interface gives you no switch for it.

You want to turn that reporting off through the app's settings.
skipWhen: You use the app in a browser rather than the desktop app.
You do not mind the desktop app reporting usage events.

The place events are sent can be overridden by a setting

A desktop launch that fails before the app is ready cannot report that launch

name: dsh-client-resources
catalogDescription: Unified client resource model: protocol-registered providers turn URL addresses into live values, consumed through the useResource global standard hook
manifestDescription: Unified client resource model: protocol-registered providers turn URL addresses into live values, consumed through the useResource global standard hook

readme.description: Client resource model: protocol-registered providers turn URL addresses into live values that any slot component reads through the useResource standard hook.
readme.summary: Use client resources when a component knows live data only by URL address, such as a tab record, link, or mention, while another client package owns the data. Resource addresses use `dsh-resource://<type>/…`; protocols that need a scope encode it in the path. Components receive the current value and later updates through the public `useResource` hook. Unsupported protocols and non-resource schemes, such as `sidebar://guide`, resolve to no resource.

rationale: Unified resource model: protocol providers behind the useResource hook.

plain.headline: Share live data across the page
plain.oneLiner: Turns an address into live data that parts of the page can share.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives parts of the page a standard way to turn an address into live data, so a tab record, link, or mention can show the current value. Unsupported addresses show nothing.
plain.whyYoudCare: Mostly for plugin authors; for you it is the plumbing behind links and mentions that show live content.
useWhen: You are building a page component that follows a link or a record.
You want several parts of the page to receive the same live value.
skipWhen: You are not building anything for the interface.
pros: One standard hook reads live values from any part of the page
Address kinds it does not understand resolve to nothing instead of failing
Every part of the page that renders receives it, whatever its place
cons: A record stays in the page's memory for the life of the page, so memory grows with addresses read
Stopping work when a reader leaves is up to each provider, not enforced here

name: dsh-client-shortcuts
catalogDescription: Application keyboard command registry and physical-key routing
manifestDescription: Application keyboard command registry and physical-key routing

readme.description: Customize application keyboard commands for each device
readme.summary:
Customize application keyboard commands for each device. Desktop and Web choose separate defaults for the receiving device. Custom bindings survive reloads on the same device. Commands disappear when their owning plugin unloads, while their saved overrides remain available for reinstallation.

Windows uses ` + ` between modifiers and the first ordinary key. Two simultaneous ordinary keys appear side by side, such as `F G`, on Windows and macOS Desktop, including tooltips and the shortcut reference.

plain.headline: Change the app's keyboard shortcuts
plain.oneLiner: Lets you rebind app commands per device, and keeps your bindings across reloads.

plain.whyYoudCare: Use it when a default combination clashes with your browser or system, or you would rather use another key.
useWhen: A shortcut does not fire because your browser or system takes it first.
You want a command on a different key on this device.
skipWhen: The default keys already suit you.
Your shortcut is one the operating system never hands to the window.
pros: Custom bindings are remembered per device and survive reloads
Desktop and web pick their own defaults for the device receiving the keys
Labels, keycaps, and conflicts all live in one place you can see
Overrides are kept even when the plugin that owns a command is removed
cons: Shortcuts the operating system never passes to the window cannot be caught
A two-key combination does not hold its first key, so a system action or focus change can break it
Registering or removing a command discards any open edit draft, even if your saved choices did not change
On desktop the shortcut file is reread on every update, with no watcher

readme.summary: Manage active and inactive tasks from the Automation tasks page and the right Sidebar task tab: search, filter, edit name, instruction, and run time, browse records, delete, or open the original conversation. Every surface names a task by its title. An open Session's header shows an icon-only reminder clock while active reminders exist and opens that task's detail; a `schedule_create` call renders a transcript card; an idle, unarchived Session row with active tasks shows a clock mark and hover list.

plain.headline: Schedule tasks and reminders
plain.oneLiner: Manage scheduled tasks and reminders after switching on an optional add-on pack.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds an Automation tasks page and a task tab in the sidebar where you can search, rename, edit, and delete scheduled tasks, with a reminder clock on sessions that have them.
plain.whyYoudCare: It lets you set a reminder or a repeating job once instead of asking for it again every time.
useWhen: You want a reminder or task to run later or on a repeat.
You want to review or clean up tasks you set up earlier.
You want to reopen the conversation a task came from.
skipWhen: You do not want anything running on a schedule.
You would rather not switch on an experimental add-on pack.
pros: Search the task list and filter it by status
Edit a task's name, instruction, and run time
Open the original conversation behind a task
cons: It is not switched on in this build; you must enable an experimental add-on pack first
Deleting a reminder does not stop one that is already queued to run
New reminders are created by asking the model, not from a form on the page
Old prompt text and earlier records cannot be recovered once they are pruned
Pausing a task or running it immediately is not available

name: dsh-client-ui-session
catalogDescription: Session Controller adapter for React and session-scoped slots
manifestDescription: Session Controller adapter for React and session-scoped slots

readme.description: React and Slot adapters for Session Controller lists, interaction state, and per-session context.
readme.summary:
Use this package to expose Session catalog, retain information, and unified UI status through standard Slot hooks. It materializes per-`SessionBinding` hooks and props, while `SessionProvider` can inherit an outer binding or bind an explicit `SessionReference`. It owns process-local pending-interaction and completion-reminder policy without owning Controller transport, history, or references.

Running status comes from Host list baselines or status events. Subagent catalog rows and retained subagent fallback rows do not establish running status; main view references still acknowledge completions.

plain.headline: Session details for the interface
plain.oneLiner: Internal glue that hands each screen the open conversation's details.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal piece that gives each screen the open conversation's details and status, so panels can show what is running and what is waiting on you.
plain.whyYoudCare: It works underneath the screens you already use, and there is nothing for you to set up.
useWhen: You are building a web feature that needs details about the open conversation.
skipWhen: You only use the app as it ships.
pros: Running status comes from the app's own reports rather than guesswork
Waiting questions and completion reminders are handled in one place
A screen can inherit the outer conversation or bind one of its own
cons: A waiting question is held in the page, so a reconnect may need it sent again
Entries for helper agents and retained fallbacks do not count as running status

name: dsh-client-ui-settings
catalogDescription: Settings domain base plugin: shared configuration forms and the canonical settings slot-type contract
manifestDescription: Settings domain base plugin: shared configuration forms and the canonical settings slot-type contract

readme.description: Settings domain base plugin: shared configuration forms, schema service, and the canonical settings slot-type contract for the dsh web client.
readme.summary: This package lets web-client features expose editable preferences backed by the Host settings document without implementing their own transport or schema handling. Each feature gets namespace-scoped reads and writes, atomic multi-field updates, schema validation, and protection against silently overwriting concurrent changes. It also provides the standard extension points for settings chrome, pages, header actions, plugin tabs, and onboarding while rendering no interface itself. Any preference-owning feature can use it without depending on a presentation package; a separate package provides the settings shell.

plain.headline: Shared settings storage for features
plain.oneLiner: Internal helper that stores and checks the preferences features save.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that lets features store and edit your preferences safely, checking the values and stopping two changes from overwriting each other. It draws no interface itself.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is already at work behind the settings pages you open, and you never need to touch it.
useWhen: You are adding a feature that needs to save a preference.
skipWhen: You only change settings through the pages that already exist.
pros: Features save preferences without writing their own storage code
Two changes at once cannot silently overwrite each other
Values are checked before they are saved
cons: Settings are not saved when you open the app from an address other than this machine; the form shows as unavailable there

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-account
catalogDescription: Manage DeepSeek login and open Platform billing pages
manifestDescription: Manage DeepSeek login and open Platform billing pages

readme.description: Desktop Account settings display DeepSeek login state and offer browser authorization and cancellation; the sidebar account menu provides Platform sign-out.
readme.summary: The Account settings section displays DeepSeek login state and offers browser sign-in and cancellation; the sidebar account menu provides Platform sign-out. Desktop users also receive a resumable introduction to account credit and presentation preferences.

rationale:
Configuration-surface reads and writes over Typert Remote. Each method
reports an actionable error when its settings-domain provider is absent.

plain.headline: Sign in to your DeepSeek account
plain.oneLiner: Sign in to DeepSeek and reach credit and billing from the desktop app.
plain.whatItDoes: Shows your DeepSeek sign-in state in Settings, lets you sign in or cancel and sign out from the sidebar menu, and opens the billing pages on the DeepSeek Platform site.
plain.whyYoudCare: It connects the desktop app to your DeepSeek account so credit and billing sit alongside your other settings.
useWhen: You want to sign in to or out of your DeepSeek account.
You want to check your credit or open billing.
You use the desktop app and want the account introduction.
skipWhen: You use the app in a browser, where this section does not appear.
You would rather work with an access key alone.
pros: Sign in and sign out from the sidebar
The page refreshes when you open it and after you sign in or reconnect
A failed lookup is shown as a failure instead of a zero balance
cons: It only appears in the desktop app, not in a plain browser
Billing and top-up open on the DeepSeek Platform site in your browser
Notice text can keep an old language until you refresh the page
While the Platform view is open, desktop menus stay visible but cannot be used

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-agent-loop
catalogDescription: Settings page of the agent loop on the dsh web client's Plugins page: the parallel tool-call cap of the agent-loop namespace
manifestDescription: Settings page of the agent loop on the dsh web client's Plugins page: the parallel tool-call cap of the agent-loop namespace

readme.description: The agent loop's settings page on the dsh web client's Plugins page: the parallel tool-call cap of the agent-loop namespace.
readme.summary: Open **Plugins** in the sidebar and select **Agent loop** in the Official group to set how many parallel-safe tool calls one step may run at once. The page stages what is typed and writes it only on save, marks a value the user overrode, and offers to reset it to the deployment's default. The page exists while the Host serves the `agent-loop` namespace.

plain.headline: Set how many tools run at once
plain.oneLiner: One setting for how many tool calls a single step may run at once.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds an Agent loop settings page with one field: how many tool calls one step may run at the same time. It marks a value you changed and lets you put the shipped default back.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the one control for how much happens at the same time during a single step.
useWhen: You want a step to run more tool calls at once.
You want to return the limit to the shipped default.
skipWhen: You are happy with the default behaviour.
pros: Nothing is saved until you press Save, so a stray keystroke does nothing
A changed value is marked as overridden and can be reset
The field shows the value currently in force
cons: This page holds this one setting only; the team of agents is fixed when the app starts
Text that is not a number blocks the save and is flagged under the field
Leaving the page throws away an unsaved change

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-general
catalogDescription: Settings ownerless-copy and product onboarding plugin: the General section, shell trigger/header chrome content, settings dictionaries, and the versioned welcome notice
manifestDescription: Settings ownerless-copy and product onboarding plugin: the General section, shell trigger/header chrome content, settings dictionaries, and the versioned welcome notice

readme.description: Settings shell, ownerless copy, and durable product-onboarding namespace for the dsh web client: the General section, trigger chrome, and onboarding ledger projection.
readme.summary: Use this package to give the dsh web client a Settings panel, connection-recovery control, feature-contributed navigation, and sequential first-run onboarding. Users can open it from the sidebar, retry a failed connection immediately, and access a local configuration file when the Host makes one available on a loopback browser. Feature packages supply their own settings rows, sections, and onboarding steps; this package supplies their shared presentation and the Coding Tools switch without adding onboarding copy.

plain.headline: Gives the app its Settings panel
plain.oneLiner: The Settings panel, the connection retry control, and the first-run steps.
plain.whatItDoes: Provides the Settings panel and the sidebar control that opens it, the retry control for a dropped connection, and the shared frame that other features add their pages and first-run steps to.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the door to every preference in the app and the control you reach for when the connection drops.
useWhen: You want to change a preference.
The app says it is disconnected and you want to retry now.
You are going through the first-run steps.
skipWhen: You never change settings.
You prefer to let a dropped connection recover on its own.
pros: The Settings control is reachable whether the sidebar is open or collapsed
A retry starts immediately and the connection state is named plainly
Other features add their own pages and steps to the same frame
cons: Most entries on the General page come from other features, so this part supplies only a few
On Windows, the update badge bubble can be covered by the desktop menu when the sidebar is collapsed

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-models
catalogDescription: Models settings and shared product-onboarding dialogs over existing settings and credential joins
manifestDescription: Models settings and shared product-onboarding dialogs over existing settings and credential joins

readme.description: Models settings and product-onboarding plugin for the dsh web client: provider rows, API-key management, model lists, and the DeepSeek first-run dialogs.
readme.summary: `dsh-client-ui-settings-models` is the Models settings page of the dsh web client: users configure API keys (stored write-only under the profile's credential reference), edit each provider's model list, and hand-declare custom pi-ai routes, with provider rows and one editor card at a time. The page joins the provider directory, the settings document, and the credential descriptions into one shared snapshot, so a row's state stays consistent across all three. It also walks first-run users through two ordered dialogs — a versioned preview notice and the conditional official-DeepSeek credential step.

plain.headline: Add your AI service access keys
plain.oneLiner: Enter access keys and choose which models each AI service offers.
plain.whatItDoes: The Models settings page: store access keys for each AI service, edit the list of models a service offers, and declare a custom route by hand, with one editor card open at a time.
plain.whyYoudCare: This is where you put the key that lets the assistant use a particular AI service.
useWhen: You need to paste an access key for a service.
You want to change which models a service offers.
You are setting the app up for the first time.
skipWhen: Your keys are already configured and working.
You use whatever the installation already provides.
pros: Keys are stored write-only and are never shown back to you
All three views of a service come from one snapshot, so its status stays consistent
Removing an entry deletes only a key it can prove belongs to that entry
cons: Only the access key and a few curated fields are editable here; retry rules and timeouts live in a configuration file
You can hand-declare a custom route for only one kind of AI service
Service names appear as internal identifiers, with no friendly names and no search
A service whose models cannot be read must have its models entered by hand

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-plugin-inventory
catalogDescription: Read-only Cordis Loader inventory tab in Web Plugins settings
manifestDescription: Read-only Cordis Loader inventory tab in Web Plugins settings

readme.description: Scope-grouped read-only plugin inventory tab in Web Plugins settings for the dsh web client: agent-preset compositions first, the global plane behind a disclosure, search across both.
readme.summary: The **Plugin list** tab lets Web users inspect plugins without changing their configuration. It lists agent presets, open by default, then the collapsed global inventory; a search opens both. Cards show localized titles and descriptions when available, identify instances by stable entry id, and expose enablement, source details, runtime status, disabled conditions, and discovery failures; preset-provided global entries name their presets. Search covers both groups and points to matches in other presets. The tab handles loading, empty, no-match, failure, and retry states without exposing transport details, and still shows the global inventory without a preset roster.

rationale:
Read-only Plugin list tab in the Settings Plugins section; the built-in
bundles the sidebar page leaves out are inspected here.

plain.headline: See every plugin and what state it is in
plain.oneLiner: A read-only list of every plugin, showing what is on and what failed to load.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds a Plugin list tab to Settings that shows every plugin your build knows about, whether each one is switched on, where it came from, and any problem found while loading it. You can search the list and open the groups that start collapsed.
plain.whyYoudCare: When an install fails or a feature goes missing, this list tells you what is loaded, what is off, and what went wrong.
useWhen: You want to check whether a particular plugin is switched on.
An install failed and you want to approve its build steps and retry.
A feature is missing and you want to find out why.
skipWhen: You want to change settings for a plugin you already know about.
You want to switch a plugin on or off; this tab only reports what it finds.
pros: You can look around without any risk of changing your setup.
It names the cause when a plugin is switched off or fails to load.
Search covers every group and points you to matches in other places.
A failed install offers one click to approve the listed build steps and retry.
cons: It takes one snapshot when you open Settings and will not refresh on its own.
Switching tabs keeps that same snapshot; only reopening Settings gets a newer one.
You cannot switch a plugin on or off here; it only reports.

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-plugins
catalogDescription: Built-in plugins settings section for the dsh web client: the Settings navigation entry and the tab chrome feature-owned tabs register into
manifestDescription: Built-in plugins settings section for the dsh web client: the Settings navigation entry and the tab chrome feature-owned tabs register into

readme.description: Built-in plugins settings section for the dsh web client: the Settings navigation entry and the tab chrome that feature-owned tabs register into.
readme.summary: Use the **Built-in plugins** settings section to inspect the plugins this deployment ships. The section is a shell: it owns the navigation entry and the tab row, and every tab in it is registered by another plugin — the read-only inventory ships one. Configuring a built-in plugin happens on the sidebar's Plugins page, where each official plugin's own companion package registers its page.

rationale:
The Built-in plugins settings section: the navigation entry and the tab
row the inventory tab registers into. The official configuration pages
are the companion rows below.

plain.headline: The Built-in plugins part of Settings
plain.oneLiner: The Settings section that holds the pages for the plugins your build ships.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds the Built-in plugins section to Settings, with its navigation entry and the bar of tabs inside it. The tabs come from other plugins, so the section can show an empty line when none has registered.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the way into the settings pages this build ships, though on its own it gives you nothing to change.
useWhen: You want to reach the settings pages for the plugins your build includes.
You are wondering why a section in Settings looks empty.
skipWhen: You never open Settings; nothing here affects your work.
You would rather configure a plugin from the Plugins page in the sidebar.
pros: It gives the settings pages of the shipped plugins one home.
Pages added by other plugins appear here on their own.
The empty state is plain about there being nothing to show.
cons: The section has no page of its own and shows an empty line until a plugin adds a tab.
Changing a built-in plugin's settings still happens on the Plugins page in the sidebar.

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-session-log
catalogDescription: General settings control for Session-log upload with DeepSeek API requests
manifestDescription: General settings control for Session-log upload with DeepSeek API requests

readme.description: Control Session-log upload with DeepSeek API requests from General settings.
readme.summary: Use **Upload Session Log when using the official model API** above the version number in **Settings → General** to control Session-log upload with DeepSeek API requests. The switch shows the accepted Host setting and saves each change immediately. It appears only while the Host exposes the upload setting; read-only clients cannot change it.

plain.headline: Choose whether session logs are uploaded
plain.oneLiner: A switch for whether your session logs go out with requests to the official service.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds a switch above the version number in Settings, General. It decides whether your session logs are sent along with requests to the official model service, and every change saves straight away.
plain.whyYoudCare: If you want to allow or stop your sessions being logged with requests to the official service, this switch is the one place to do it.
useWhen: You want your sessions logged with the official service to help diagnose problems.
You want to stop those logs being sent.
skipWhen: You do not use the official model service.
Your build does not offer this setting, in which case the switch stays hidden.
pros: One switch, saved the moment you change it.
It shows the value the service actually accepted.
If a save fails, the old value stays and a message tells you, even after you close Settings.
cons: The switch is missing when your build does not offer this setting.
A client without write access cannot change it.

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-shell
catalogDescription: Settings page of the shell executor on the dsh web client's Plugins page: the command timeout and the per-stream output cap of the shell namespace
manifestDescription: Settings page of the shell executor on the dsh web client's Plugins page: the command timeout and the per-stream output cap of the shell namespace

readme.description: The shell executor's settings page on the dsh web client's Plugins page: the command timeout and the per-stream output cap of the shell namespace.
readme.summary: Open **Plugins** in the sidebar and select **Shell** in the Official group to set how long one command may run and how much of each output stream stays in memory. The page stages what is typed and writes it only on save, marks the values the user overrode, and offers to reset each back to the deployment's default. The page exists while the Host serves the `shell` namespace, so a deployment without a local shell executor shows no trace of it.

rationale:
The official settings pages: one companion package per host-plane
namespace, each registering its page into the Plugins page while the
Host serves the namespace.

plain.headline: Set the command time limit and output size
plain.oneLiner: Sets how long a command may run and how much output is kept.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds a Shell page under Plugins. It sets how long one command may run before it is stopped, and how much of each output stream is kept in memory before the rest spills to a temporary file.
plain.whyYoudCare: When a long-running or very talkative command gets cut short or spills to a file, these are the two values that decide it.
useWhen: A command you rely on keeps being stopped for taking too long.
Output is spilling to a file and you want to raise the limit.
skipWhen: Your build has no local shell, in which case the page never appears.
You are happy with the defaults; nothing here needs your attention.
pros: Both values start at the deployment default, so you change only what you need.
Fields you have overridden are marked and can be reset in one click.
Nothing is saved until you press Save, so leaving the page changes nothing.
cons: Only the time limit and the output cap are editable here.
A setting that exists on one platform and not another is not offered on this page.

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-subagent
catalogDescription: Settings page of Subagent delegation on the dsh web client's Plugins page: recursion depth, parallel capacity, and the models agents may choose for subagents
manifestDescription: Settings page of Subagent delegation on the dsh web client's Plugins page: recursion depth, parallel capacity, and the models agents may choose for subagents

readme.description: The Subagent settings page on the dsh web client's Plugins page: delegation depth and capacity over the subagent namespace, and the models agents may choose over subagent-model-selection, on one page with one save.
readme.summary: Open **Plugins** in the sidebar and select **Subagent** in the Official group to set how deep and how wide delegation may go, and which models agents may choose for their subagents. The page groups the two Host namespaces, `subagent` and `subagent-model-selection`, under one save; it exists while the Host serves either and shows the sections it serves.

plain.headline: Control how deep and wide helpers may go
plain.oneLiner: Sets how deep helpers may nest, how many run at once, and their models.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds a Subagent page under Plugins. It sets how many levels of helpers a helper may start, how many helpers may run at once under one main agent, and which models agents may hand to the helpers they start.
plain.whyYoudCare: Delegation can fan out quickly, so these limits and the allowed models are how you keep it predictable.
useWhen: You want to stop helpers from nesting many levels deep.
You want to cap how many helpers run at the same time.
You want to decide which models assistants may pick for their helpers.
skipWhen: You never use helpers.
The limits your build already ships with are fine for you.
pros: Depth and capacity sit side by side, each with its rule explained behind an information button.
One save covers both groups of settings on the page.
Models your build stored but no service currently offers stay listed and can still be removed.
A service that fails to load offers a retry without hiding the others.
cons: The list of available models refreshes only on a few events, or when you press the retry button.
A service that starts offering models between those events will not show up until the next one.

name: dsh-client-ui-settings-web-search
catalogDescription: Settings page of the DeepSeek web-search provider on the dsh web client's Plugins page: its API key, endpoint, and per-request search budget
manifestDescription: Settings page of the DeepSeek web-search provider on the dsh web client's Plugins page: its API key, endpoint, and per-request search budget

readme.description: The DeepSeek web-search provider's settings page on the dsh web client's Plugins page: its API key, endpoint, and per-request search budget.
readme.summary: Open **Plugins** in the sidebar and select **Web search** in the Official group to set the provider's key, endpoint, and how many times one request may search. The page stages what is typed and writes it only on save; the key is written through the credentials domain rather than the settings document, so its literal never rides a response. The page exists while the Host serves the `web-search-deepseek` namespace.

plain.headline: Set the web search key, address, and budget
plain.oneLiner: Sets the web search key, the address to call, and how many searches are allowed.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds a Web search page under Plugins. It sets the key used to search the web, which address to call, and how many searches one request may make. The key is stored apart from the page and is never sent back to it.
plain.whyYoudCare: Without a key of your own, only conversations on a DeepSeek Account model can search, and only through the default address.
useWhen: You want web search to work with your own key.
You want search to call a different address.
You want to limit how many searches one request may make.
skipWhen: You only chat with a DeepSeek Account model, where search already works.
Your build does not offer this page, in which case it stays hidden.
pros: The key is never sent back to the page, only whether one is set.
It says plainly when search is limited to account models.
Overridden values are marked and can be reset to the default.
cons: The search model, API version, and text budget cannot be changed here.
If the key comes from the environment, the field is disabled.
Nothing is written until you press Save, so an unsaved key does nothing.

name: dsh-client-ui-shortcuts
catalogDescription: Keyboard shortcut reference, recording, and local preference editing
manifestDescription: Keyboard shortcut reference, recording, and local preference editing

readme.description: Browse the commands available in the current window and find them by action, English alias, or key
readme.summary: Browse the commands available in the current window and find them by action, English alias, or key. Open the reference from General Settings or Mod+/. Record, clear, or restore application bindings; fixed input actions remain read-only.

plain.headline: See and change your keyboard shortcuts
plain.oneLiner: A window for finding, rebinding, and resetting keyboard shortcuts.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds a Keyboard shortcuts window you can open from General Settings or with Mod+/. It lists the commands available here, lets you search them by name or key, and lets you record, clear, or restore a key.
plain.whyYoudCare: If a key combination clashes with another program, this is where you move it without editing any files.
useWhen: You want to find which key runs a particular action.
A shortcut clashes with another program and you want to change it.
You want to undo your changes and go back to the defaults.
skipWhen: You are happy with the keys your build ships with.
You want to change a key for a fixed action; those stay read-only.
pros: You can find a command by name, by its English alias, or by the keys themselves.
Recording, clearing, and restoring all happen in one window.
Your changes stay on your machine, so they do not affect anyone else.
cons: Recording reads physical key positions and uses US-layout names, so other layouts can surprise you.
Which key combinations a browser allows is limited by the shortcut service.
If commands are loaded or unloaded while you are recording, your draft is dropped and you start again.

name: dsh-client-ui-sidebar
catalogDescription: Sidebar plugin: session multi-level tree, search, grouping, state dots
manifestDescription: Sidebar plugin: session multi-level tree, search, grouping, state dots

readme.description: Sidebar shell plugin for the dsh web client: brand row, New Session action, collapse control, scroll-aware region seat, and bottom-pinned Settings seat.
readme.summary: The dsh web client sidebar lets users recognize the active build, start a new session, collapse navigation to a 56px rail, browse Workspaces and Sessions, and open Settings. It preserves a bottom-pinned Settings entry and hides idle scrollbars without moving browser rows. New Session uses an explicitly selected Workspace, then the current Session's Workspace, then the most recently active Workspace; if none exists, it opens a blank New Session page. Deployments can replace the brand mark or name while retaining the navigation controls and rail geometry.

plain.headline: The navigation column down the left side
plain.oneLiner: The left column for starting sessions, moving between them, and reaching Settings.
plain.whatItDoes: Draws the left-hand column where you see which build you are using, start a new session, browse your workspaces and sessions, and reach Settings. You can fold it down to a narrow strip to give the conversation more room.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how you move around: switching sessions, opening Settings, or starting something new.
useWhen: You want to move between sessions or workspaces.
You want more reading space and fold the column away.
You want to start a new session in a workspace you choose.
skipWhen: You only ever use one session; there is little to navigate.
You are looking for session status dots or grouping controls, which come from a companion plugin.
pros: Folding it to a narrow strip keeps navigation in reach while freeing space.
The Settings entry stays pinned at the bottom.
A new session opens in a sensible workspace without you picking one every time.
cons: Session status dots come from a companion plugin, not this one.
Grouping, ordering, and searching your workspaces belong to that companion too.
The marker for a finished task is kept only on your machine.

name: dsh-client-ui-sidebar-browser
catalogDescription: Sandboxed Web browser tabs for the right Sidebar
manifestDescription: Sandboxed Web browser tabs for the right Sidebar

readme.description: Right-Sidebar browser tabs for sandboxed HTTP(S) pages, including loopback services.
readme.summary: Browse HTTP(S) pages, including loopback services, inside independent right-Sidebar tabs. Web uses an iframe with application-managed history; Desktop uses Electron `<webview>` with native navigation history and retained pages. The package never injects Electron or Node access into visited content.

rationale: Web profiles opt in; Desktop retains sandboxed HTTP(S) Browser tabs.

plain.headline: Open a web page beside your conversation
plain.oneLiner: A browser kept apart from the app, sitting in the right-hand sidebar.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds tabs to the right-hand sidebar that load web pages, including services running on your own machine. Visited pages are kept apart from the rest of the app and are not given access to your files or the app itself.
plain.whyYoudCare: You can read a page or check a local service next to the session that refers to it, without leaving the app.
useWhen: You want a web page open beside the session that mentions it.
You want to check a service running on your own computer.
A page is easier to read in a side panel than in another browser tab.
skipWhen: The site refuses to be shown inside another app; use your normal browser instead.
You want to preview a file on disk, which the document preview handles.
The page needs downloads or to take over the whole window.
pros: Pages stay beside the session instead of in a separate browser.
Visited pages do not get access to your files or to the app.
Each tab keeps its own page and its own place in the history.
cons: Many sites refuse to be shown this way and will not load.
Downloads and taking over the whole window are blocked by default, so some pages break.
Turning that protection off gives a page far more reach, including control of the app.
Pages in different tabs are not kept apart from one another's cookies, and a page can pick where it goes next.
When a page fails the app often cannot say why; restarting does not restore page memory or unsaved forms.

name: dsh-client-ui-sidebar-documentpreview
catalogDescription: Extensible Sidebar previews for Office documents, spreadsheets, Markdown, code, images, PDF, HTML, and plain text
manifestDescription: Extensible Sidebar previews for Office documents, spreadsheets, Markdown, code, images, PDF, HTML, and plain text

readme.summary: `dsh-client-ui-theme` lets Web GUI users choose `light`, `dark`, or `system` and set conversation content text from 10 to 22 px in Settings. A loopback client stores both values in the `ui-theme` settings namespace, which the local provider persists in `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` by default. The plugin resolves `system` through `prefers-color-scheme` and publishes immutable `ThemeSnapshot`s; ui-layout applies each snapshot to the document. The package also ships the `--dsw-*` token stylesheets and injects a synchronous bootstrap so the selected palette and font size apply before the shell loads. Third-party themes can register alias-token overrides through `ctx.theme`.

name: dsh-client-ui-tool

readme.description: Client Tool presentation plugin for the dsh web client: whole-call tree composition, the keyed per-tool view slot, and the built-in atomic tool cards.
readme.summary: `dsh-client-ui-tool` is the client Tool presentation plugin of the dsh web client: it renders every tool call in the conversation. `ui-conversation` dispatches each ordered `tool-call` Conversation Node through the matching key of `conversation.chat.node`; this package renders its root and PTC dispatch children, then dispatches every atomic call through the keyed `tool.call.toolview` slot. Unregistered Tool names use the generic card. Business UI packages register only their wire Tool names and atomic views — they do not pair Session events, rebuild the transcript, or own root/subcall topology, because the Runtime remains authoritative for call/result pairing, lifecycle, and recursive `subCalls` projection.

rationale: Tool call tree, generic fallback, and keyed business Tool views.

plain.headline: How actions appear in the chat
plain.oneLiner: Draws each action the assistant takes as a card with its steps and status.
plain.whatItDoes: Draws every action the assistant takes as a card in the conversation: a main action with its nested steps, live status, and a plain card for anything unusual.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how you follow what the assistant is actually doing and spot a failure while it happens.
useWhen: You want to watch the assistant work step by step.
You want to see which action failed and why.

You want links inside those cards to follow your usual link setting.

cons: Web links in these cards always open a new browser tab, ignoring your link setting.
Some actions cannot run nested code in this mode, so you may see only one level.
Actions without their own card fall back to a generic one.

Closing a card linked to a tool call hides it; its tool row reopens it and later shows recorded answers. Durable workflow lifecycle as an independent Chat node after the

name: dsh-command-compact

manifestDescription: Human-facing slash command for explicit session compaction

readme.description: The on-demand /compact command for interactive compositions: what it does, what you see, and how to mount it.
readme.summary: `dsh-command-compact` adds a `/compact` command to chat UIs: type it and the conversation condenses on demand — the older history is replaced by one summary even before automatic pressure triggers. The command works with any condensation backend and does not consume a model turn; after it finishes you see how many history items were condensed and the estimated tokens saved. While the agent is mid-turn or condensation is already running, it tells you condensation is unavailable. Prompts you send while it runs stay queued and start after it finishes.

rationale:

independent, so it follows whichever compaction service this leaf mounts.

plain.whyYoudCare: On a long conversation you can clear room at a moment you choose instead of waiting for the assistant to run out of space.

You want to see how many items were condensed and how many text was saved.

You are happy to let condensation happen automatically.

It works with whichever condensation backend is running
It does not use up a model turn

Typing `/feedback` plus a remark records it and acknowledges the session and anonymous user ids; the Web feedback dialog records a category and an optional description through the `sessionFeedback` Host Remote. Recording is immediate and never starts model work: the model neither sees the remark nor is interrupted by it. The package also owns the fixed category taxonomy every feedback surface files under. It ships with the standard `dsh` base and needs no configuration; headless, ACP, and JSON-RPC entry points provide no slash commands.

manifestDescription: Human-facing slash command for persisted same-session goals

readme.summary: `dsh-command-goal` gives users the `/goal` command to create, edit, pause, resume, clear, and inspect the current goal directly in an interactive UI. The goal service and session driver stay on the host plane, where Gateway

readme.description: Automatic conversation condensation for deployments choosing, tuning, or debugging how older history is summarized as token pressure builds.
readme.summary: This package keeps long agent conversations working near the model's context limit. As token pressure builds, it condenses the oldest history into a summary while preserving recent messages; after a context-overflow error, it condenses and retries. You can also request condensation with `/compact` and optionally trim oversized tool outputs first. Condensation uses one extra model request and retains only its summary text. It cannot reduce the system prompt, tools, or session prefix, or split one indivisible unit such as a single huge tool call.

rationale:
The token METER stays on the host plane; only the compaction backend that
reads it moves. It owns the context-meter projection units, and that table is
process-wide, so preset ownership would make the meter a function of which
presets happen to be mounted rather than a per-session fact. Same criterion as
`tasks` and `goals`; the reasoning has one home in
`.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-08-10-host-plane-ownership-after-presets.md`.
