name: dsh-fs
catalogDescription: Abstract filesystem capability seam (ctx.fs) for the DeepSeek Harness — vocabulary types, the FileSystem service (text IO + optional version-guarded atomic mutations), and the fs/* policy event vocabulary
manifestDescription: Abstract filesystem capability seam (ctx.fs) for the DeepSeek Harness — vocabulary types, the FileSystem service (text IO + optional version-guarded atomic mutations), and the fs/* policy event vocabulary

readme.description: The ctx.fs filesystem service contract for deployments choosing or mounting a filesystem backend and developers implementing one.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-fs` when an application needs consistent filesystem operations across host, confined, or remote execution environments. It lets consumers resolve stable file identities, map shared host files where supported, perform bounded text and byte reads, list directories, watch targets, and apply atomic text writes and literal edits. Version guards are optional, so a backend works without policy enforcement; callers can supply a guard to reject a mutation after the file changes. Choose `fs-local` or `fs-sandbox` for host execution. Model-facing filesystem tools are provided separately by `dsh-tool-fs`.

headings.text: What the service lets you do

plain.headline: Shared way to read and write files
plain.oneLiner: Internal helper for reading and writing files. Nothing for you to configure.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that gives the rest of the software one consistent way to read, list, and write files, wherever those files live. There is nothing here for you to configure.

name: dsh-fs-local
catalogDescription: Local-filesystem implementation of the DeepSeek Harness filesystem seam (ctx.fs)
manifestDescription: Local-filesystem implementation of the DeepSeek Harness filesystem seam (ctx.fs)

readme.description: The host-filesystem backend for ctx.fs for deployments and maintainers choosing or debugging local file access.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-fs-local` to read, list, watch, atomically write, and edit files on the host filesystem. Relative paths resolve from a configurable base directory, while absolute paths and parent traversal remain unrestricted. Paths and symlinks that reach the same file share one identity. Writes preserve file permissions, and optional version guards reject stale overwrites. Choose this package for direct host access; use `fs-sandbox` for confined mutations.

plain.headline: Read and write files on this machine
plain.oneLiner: A developer building block for direct, unrestricted file access on this machine.
plain.whatItDoes: A building block that gives the software direct access to files on the machine it runs on: reading, listing, watching, writing and editing them. It is the unrestricted counterpart to the confined file access used by default.
plain.whyYoudCare: It only matters if you are putting together your own setup and need plain, unconfined access to this machine's files.
useWhen: You are assembling a setup that needs unrestricted access to this machine's files.
You want file changes to keep the permissions a file already had.
skipWhen: You want the assistant's changes confined to your project folder, which the confined option already does.
You need changes held inside a folder: the base directory here is a starting point, not a fence.
pros: Reading, listing, watching, writing and editing files all live in one place
Writes preserve the permissions a file already had
Optional guards reject an overwrite of something that changed since it was read
Two paths that reach the same file are treated as one file
cons: Its base directory does not contain anything: absolute paths and .. climb straight out of it
Editing a file holds the whole file and the edited copy in memory
The stale-overwrite guard depends on file timestamps and identifiers that some storage layers never update
Binary detection is uneven: a file with a late null byte reads fine but refuses edits
The lock that serialises two changes to the same file applies only within one process

name: dsh-fs-observation-policy
catalogDescription: File-context policy plugin for the DeepSeek Harness — observed-state, read-before-edit, and version-guarded write/edit added over the ctx.fs provider seam through the fs/* event gate (no service API)
manifestDescription: File-context policy plugin for the DeepSeek Harness — observed-state, read-before-edit, and version-guarded write/edit added over the ctx.fs provider seam through the fs/* event gate (no service API)

readme.description: The read-before-edit filesystem policy plugin for deployments and maintainers choosing or debugging guarded write and edit behavior.
readme.summary: `dsh-fs-observation-policy` makes filesystem tools require an agent to read a file before overwriting or editing it. It also rejects a mutation when the file has changed since that read, and returns a clear instruction to re-read and retry. Reading a missing path authorizes guarded creation, while concurrent creation remains protected. Choose it for deployments that want read-before-write safety; resumed sessions must read targets again because observations are not persisted.

plain.headline: Read a file before overwriting it
plain.oneLiner: Makes the assistant read a file before it may overwrite or edit it.
plain.whatItDoes: Stops the assistant overwriting or editing a file it has not read first, and refuses a change when the file has moved on since that read, telling it to read again and retry.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the reason a file is not silently replaced by content the assistant never looked at.
useWhen: You want protection against files being changed blind to what they currently contain.
You want a stale change refused and retried rather than applied.
skipWhen: Your code touches files directly instead of through the assistant's file tools, because those calls are not covered.
pros: The assistant must read a file before it can overwrite or edit it
A change is refused when the file changed since that read, with an instruction to read again
Reading a path that does not exist yet still allows a guarded new file
It needs no settings, so there is nothing for you to fill in
cons: The record of what has been read does not survive resuming a session, so files must be read again
Anything without its own session can never satisfy the rule and cannot overwrite an existing file at all
A file read outside the assistant's read tool stays unrecorded, so a later edit is rejected
A partial read is enough to authorise replacing the whole file when nothing has changed since

name: dsh-fs-sandbox
catalogDescription: Sandbox-enforcing implementation of the DeepSeek Harness filesystem seam: fences write/edit by the per-call sandbox mode (read-only denies mutation, workspace-write contains it to the workspace + temp roots) while reads pass through
manifestDescription: Sandbox-enforcing implementation of the DeepSeek Harness filesystem seam: fences write/edit by the per-call sandbox mode (read-only denies mutation, workspace-write contains it to the workspace + temp roots) while reads pass through

readme.description: The sandbox-enforcing ctx.fs backend for deployments and maintainers confining model file mutations to a session workspace.
readme.summary: `dsh-fs-sandbox` confines model file writes and edits according to each session's sandbox mode while preserving the local filesystem's read behavior. In `read-only`, it rejects every mutation; in `workspace-write`, it permits targets only inside the session workspace or a platform temporary root; in `danger-full-access`, it does not restrict mutations. Use it instead of `fs-local` with `ctx.sandboxPolicy` when sessions need workspace-confined file changes. Denied operations return `FS_SANDBOX_DENIED`, which filesystem tools present with the active mode and a same-turn escalation hint.

rationale:
The sandboxed filesystem provider. `cwd` defaults to `process.cwd()`; an
overlay can pin another workspace.

plain.headline: Keep the assistant's file changes in bounds
plain.oneLiner: Limits where the assistant may write files, following the session's safety mode.
plain.whatItDoes: Limits where the assistant may write or edit files, following the safety mode chosen for the session: refuse every change, allow changes only inside your workspace and a temporary area, or lift the limit.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what stops a session writing outside your project folder when the session is set to the middle mode.
useWhen: You want the assistant's file changes limited to your project and a temporary folder.
You want a mode that refuses file changes entirely for a read-only session.
skipWhen: You are running in the unrestricted mode, where no file change is confined.
You need a hard barrier against a determined program on your machine: this is a rule the tools follow.
pros: Reads are never restricted; only writing and editing are fenced
The same mode drives the file tools and the shell, so both confine to the same places
A refused change reports the active mode and a same-turn hint for asking for more
In the unrestricted mode it does not limit changes at all
cons: It is a policy check over trusted code, not an operating-system boundary, so hostile local programs are out of scope
It needs the session's safety mode to be available and confines nothing without it
The writable places come from one shared source, so a runner defining its own set could drift apart

name: dsh-goal
catalogDescription: Event-sourced same-session goal state and lifecycle service for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Event-sourced same-session goal state and lifecycle service for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The persisted same-session goal service for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging one durable completion objective per session.
readme.summary: `dsh-goal` lets one long-running completion objective persist across turns, session resume, fork, and process restarts. Users and agents can create, edit, pause, resume, complete, block, or clear it; compare-and-set updates reject stale views. A configurable round cap (256 by default) bounds automatic continuation, and blocked goals retain a stable policy code with a human-readable explanation. The package stores goal state but does not schedule work, and continuation permission remains process-local rather than durable. Choose it for one objective spanning many turns; skip it for routine single-turn work or parallel objectives.

headings.text: What survives and what does not

plain.headline: Keep one long task going across turns
plain.oneLiner: Remembers one long-running objective across turns, resumes and restarts.
plain.whatItDoes: Stores one long-running objective for a session so it survives extra turns, resuming a session, copying a session and restarting the program. You or the assistant can create, edit, pause, resume, complete, block or clear it.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how a big job keeps its direction instead of you restating it every time you come back to it.
useWhen: You have one objective that will take many rounds of work.
You want the objective to still be there after you resume the session or restart the program.
skipWhen: The work is a single question and answer.
You want several objectives running side by side.
pros: The objective survives resuming, copying a session and restarting the program
You and the assistant can pause, resume, complete, block or clear it
An update based on an out-of-date view is rejected
A round cap, 256 by default, bounds automatic continuation
A blocked objective keeps a stable code and a plain-language explanation
cons: It stores state only; it does not decide when to continue, retry or cancel
The cap counts rounds, not text length, money, time or service quotas
There is no independent checker: whoever records completion is taken at its word
Only one objective is kept per session
A plugin with direct session access could add fake entries; a malformed record stops goal access until the log is repaired

name: dsh-goal-round-driver
catalogDescription: Race-fenced same-session goal-round driver
manifestDescription: Race-fenced same-session goal-round driver

readme.description: The same-session continuation driver for users and maintainers choosing, composing, or debugging automatic goal rounds.
readme.summary: `dsh-goal-round-driver` automatically continues an active goal in the same session while the agent is idle, continuation is armed, and the configured round allowance remains. Each round gives the model another turn toward the objective; only goal rounds that reach model history consume the allowance, and exhaustion records a blocker. The driver has no configuration: the goal defines the round limit, and `dsh-tool-goal` defines when repeated blocking stops continuation. Mount it with `dsh-goal` and `dsh-tool-goal` for unattended multi-round progress; omit it when each step requires human steering.

plain.headline: Keep a long objective moving on its own
plain.oneLiner: Runs further rounds on an active objective while the assistant sits idle.
plain.whatItDoes: Continues an active objective automatically while the assistant is idle, the continuation is switched on and rounds remain. Each round gives the assistant another turn toward the objective.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is why a long objective can make progress while you are away from the keyboard, until the round allowance runs out.
useWhen: You want an objective to keep going without you prompting every step.
skipWhen: Every step needs your judgement before the next one starts.
You want a fresh, independent attempt at the problem rather than more turns in the same session.
pros: It works on its own, with nothing to configure
Only rounds that actually reach the assistant's history use up the allowance
Running out of rounds is recorded as a blocker rather than passing silently
Stopping it disarms the objective, and no later round starts
cons: The assistant itself decides when the evidence is enough; there is no independent checker
It works only in the same session and never starts a fresh agent or an independent attempt
Stopping it is not instant: a round already accepted can begin before shutdown finishes
The round cap says nothing about tokens, money, time or service quotas
It does not retry after a temporary service or storage failure; you must resume by hand

name: dsh-headless
catalogDescription: The dsh one-shot bundle: a direct core Agent/Session runner over dsh-base with no Host, HTTP, or browser layer
manifestDescription: The dsh one-shot bundle: a direct core Agent/Session runner over dsh-base with no Host, HTTP, or browser layer

readme.description: One-shot task mode for dsh: run a single task from the command line and get the final answer printed, for users scripting or automating dsh.
readme.summary: `dsh-headless` runs one dsh task from the command line and prints the final answer, then exits — no GUI, no server, no browser. Type `dsh --profile headless "run the tests"` and the agent handles it with the same model, tools, and safety defaults as every other surface. It suits scripts, CI, and one-off jobs: it opens no ports and leaves nothing running behind. It also offers a JSON event stream (`--json`) and `--session-id` to resume a conversation. Exit code 0 means the task completed; 1 means it aborted or errored. The boundary: one task per invocation, no interactive follow-up.

plain.headline: Run one task from the command line
plain.oneLiner: Runs one task from the command line, prints the answer and exits.
plain.whatItDoes: Runs a single task from the command line and prints the final answer, then exits. No window, no server, no browser, and nothing left running afterwards.
plain.whyYoudCare: It lets you put the assistant inside a script or a build pipeline, where a program runs it and waits for a result.
useWhen: You want a step in a script or build pipeline to run the assistant.
You need a machine-readable stream of events, or to continue a conversation later by its id.
skipWhen: You want a back-and-forth conversation or a visual window.
Your task needs several rounds of you steering it before it finishes.
pros: It opens no network port and leaves nothing running behind
The model, tools and safety defaults match the other ways of running the software
An exit code of 0 means the task completed; 1 means it aborted or errored
A machine-readable event stream gives a supervisor progress, not just the final answer
A session id lets a later run continue the same conversation
cons: One task per run: the process exits once the task is answered, with no follow-up
It must be started through the dsh command; another way fails at startup
Nothing appears on the error stream until the service emits output, so a slow start looks silent
In default mode the error stream can retain a lot of the model's thinking, which may be sensitive
Default output holds only the final answer, so a run with no answer prints an empty line and exits 1

name: dsh-hmr

manifestDescription: Coordinated module and profile configuration hot reload

plain.headline: Reload changes without restarting
plain.oneLiner: Reloads plugin code and settings while the program keeps running.
plain.whatItDoes: Applies changes to plugin code and to settings while the software keeps running, so you do not have to restart it. All the kinds of change share one queue, so they are applied in order.
plain.whyYoudCare: It saves a restart every time a developer edits a plugin, and it watches source folders for edits only when someone asks for that.
useWhen: You are changing plugin code or settings and want to see the effect without restarting.
You want to switch on watching source folders for edits.
skipWhen: You are using a setup where it is switched off, such as the command-line or editor modes: changes then apply on restart.

The names and events the earlier version exposed remain available

name: dsh-home-paths
catalogDescription: Shared filesystem path helpers for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Shared filesystem path helpers for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: Shared resolution of the DeepSeek Harness home and user-data paths for packages that need one consistent root, tilde expansion, and stable watch paths.

readme.description: The provider-neutral model-call service for users and maintainers streaming requests, registering provider adapters, or resolving model metadata.
readme.summary: Use `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm` to stream model calls through configured provider adapters, discover models, and resolve model capabilities and call defaults. Callers must keep all model-visible input reconstructable from the session log. Loop-built requests arrive deep-frozen, so extensions and adapters cannot rewrite them. Each stream is one provider attempt: provider-specific translation stays with its adapter, while the optional `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-retry` package re-runs failed requests. plain.whyYoudCare: It only concerns you if you write add-ons, since everything else already reaches the AI service through it.
useWhen: You are writing an add-on that needs to call a model.
You want one place that decides which models are available.
skipWhen: You do not write add-ons; it already works quietly.
You need behaviour specific to one supplier, which lives with that supplier's own connector.
You want automatic retries, which a separate add-on provides.
pros: One shared way to call models keeps every part consistent
Requests are frozen, so add-ons cannot quietly rewrite them
Every stream ends with a clear success, failure, or cancellation result
cons: No retries, caching, or rate limiting are built in
Only a small set of tuning options is offered
Some declared message styles have nothing yet that produces them

rationale:
The pi-ai multi-provider twin, mounted dormant: zero routes (and no extra

profiles — then those routes register live, keys resolving per request
through their apiKeyEnv references, and drop again when the section empties.
Supplying those profiles is exactly what the web Models page does. Which

name: dsh-llm-retry

manifestDescription: Provider-routed LLM request retry policy for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The retry executor for users and maintainers configuring provider-routed model-request recovery at durable agent-step boundaries.
readme.summary: Mount `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-retry` to retry failed model requests at durable agent-step boundaries. Provider `retryPolicy` settings choose bounded normal-mode retries or unlimited always-mode retries; scheduled attempts reach the session log before backoff, and cancellation leaves consistent history. Retries re-run the failed step in the same open turn, while direct `ctx.llm.stream()` calls remain single-attempt. Each retry is another billed provider request, and always mode continues until success, cancellation, or disposal.

plain.headline: Retries failed requests on its own
plain.oneLiner: Tries failed model requests again with growing waits between attempts.
plain.whatItDoes: When a model request fails for a temporary reason, this tries the step again with growing waits instead of giving up. Each attempt is written to the session record before the wait begins.
plain.whyYoudCare: A brief hiccup no longer costs you the whole turn, though every retry is another billed request.
useWhen: Requests fail for rate limits, timeouts, or server trouble.
You want the assistant to recover without you repeating yourself.
skipWhen: You need tight control of cost, since each retry is billed.
You call the model directly outside the normal turn, where retries do not apply.
pros: Temporary failures are retried without you doing anything
Waits grow between attempts, giving a busy server room
Cancelling still leaves a consistent record
cons: Every retry is another billed request
Always-retry mode also retries failures that will never succeed, such as a bad key or a full quota
Only whole assistant turns can be retried, not direct model calls
An entry shows that a retry was scheduled, not that it worked

You are willing to name each program and how to start it.

The outside program needs task-style execution, which is not supported.
A slow program delaying startup would be a problem for you.

readme.description: Plan mode for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging the per-agent planning feature with deployment guidance, a /plan command, and a user-reviewed exit.
readme.summary: Plan mode asks an agent to explore and design before execution, then presents the finished plan for your approval. Enter it with `/plan`, optionally with a message or ordered image and file attachments; leave with `/plan off`, approve the review to continue, or return feedback for more planning. Deployment-defined guidance controls planning behavior, but every tool remains available, so use sandbox mode and approval prompts for enforced limits. The active state survives session resume and forks. Choose it when you want a reviewed plan before the agent acts.

headings.text: Exit tool schema and review exchange

config.section:
You are in plan mode. Stay in plan mode until exit_plan_mode succeeds or the user switches the session mode. Imperative language to implement changes means plan the implementation, not execute it. A user's conversational agreement — including an answer confirming something you asked — approves nothing and does not end plan mode; fold the confirmed decision into the plan and submit it through exit_plan_mode.

Explore first. Use non-mutating reads, searches, static analysis, and checks to ground the plan in the actual repository. Do not edit or write files, change configuration, run formatters or code generation that rewrites tracked files, commit, or otherwise carry out the plan. Prefer existing functions and patterns over new machinery.

The tool catalog stays the same across modes for request-cache stability. These plan-mode rules override any later tool description or guidance that suggests using mutation tools; those tools remain listed only to keep the request shape stable. Do not use todo_write to track this planning phase: it tracks implementation after an approved plan, while the plan itself belongs in exit_plan_mode.

Resolve discoverable facts by inspection. Use ask_user_question only for user-owned choices or material ambiguity that inspection cannot answer. Do not ask the user where code lives or how current behavior works when you can find out.

Make the plan decision-complete: state the goal and success criteria; group implementation changes by subsystem; identify public API, schema, and data-flow changes; cover edge cases, failure modes, tests, acceptance criteria, and explicit assumptions. Keep it concise enough to review but detailed enough that another engineer can implement it without making design decisions.

When ready, call exit_plan_mode with the complete plan markdown, starting with a # title. Make exit_plan_mode the only and final tool call in that assistant response: it presents the plan for approval, and implementation begins only in a later step after approval. Do not paste the final plan as a plain reply or ask "should I proceed?" through prose or ask_user_question. If review rejects it, incorporate the feedback and present again. If the review channel is unavailable or aborted, stay in plan mode and ask the user to switch modes manually; do not proceed with implementation.

readme.description: Standalone SDK profile with one default shell tool for users who need a minimal cross-platform coding agent without the shared base bundle.
readme.summary: Use `dsh --profile sdk-minimal` when an SDK client needs a small, explicit coding-agent runtime. By default, the profile advertises only a platform-selected persistent shell, persists sessions as uncompressed JSONL, and selects the model from the SDK initialization request. It supplies a complete Cordis tree and deliberately excludes `dsh-base`, Web, settings, managed credentials, telemetry, compaction, filesystem tools, workspace instructions, skills, jobs, and subagents. Its danger-full-access policy lets the shell modify any path available to the process, so use it only with an isolated workspace.

name: dsh-session
catalogDescription: Event-sourced session store for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Event-sourced session store for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The event-sourced session log and in-memory store for users and maintainers building, inspecting, or extending the durable record behind every agent interaction.
readme.summary: `dsh-session` records every model-visible fact in an append-only session log and derives model history from that record. Consumers can inspect, replay, fork, and flush sessions while preserving historical events; compaction hides superseded entries from the active conversation without deleting them. Sessions remain in memory unless a persistence backend is added, and durability checkpoints wait for configured backends. Choose this package wherever an agent needs a reconstructable session record; it does not call models.

plain.headline: The record of everything a session did
plain.oneLiner: Keeps the full ordered record of a session so it can be replayed or branched.
plain.whatItDoes: Keeps a full, append-only record of everything the assistant saw in a session and rebuilds the conversation from it. You can look back, replay, or branch a session, and replaced turns are hidden rather than erased.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what makes a session reviewable and recoverable instead of a conversation that disappears when you close it.
useWhen: You want to go back over what happened in a session.
You want to branch a session and try a different direction.
skipWhen: You expect sessions to be saved to disk by default; they stay in memory until you add storage.
You need a tree of many branches rather than one split point.
pros: Everything the assistant saw is kept in order and can be replayed.
Replaced turns are hidden from the active conversation instead of deleted.
You can branch a session at a chosen point and keep the earlier history.
cons: Sessions stay in memory unless you add a storage plugin.
Branching closes only the open end and does not fill in missing results.
There is no wider tree of branches beyond a single split.

name: dsh-session-checkpoint-policy
catalogDescription: Semantic session durability checkpoints before model requests and tool side effects
manifestDescription: Semantic session durability checkpoints before model requests and tool side effects

readme.description: Semantic session durability checkpoints for users and maintainers deploying persisted agents that must not lose a model request or tool side effect on crash.
readme.summary: Use this package with a session persistence backend to make work durable before a model request, before a top-level tool can cause external effects, and before the next agent step begins. After each checkpoint, work can resume after a crash from stored requests, tool calls, responses, and results without loss. Checkpoint failures are fail-closed: a model adapter or top-level tool body does not run until the durable write succeeds. The package has no configuration and adds no prompt or tool schema; unfinished Assistant streams remain transient, and interrupted tool calls recover with an unknown outcome instead of an automatic retry.

rationale: Durability checkpoints before each model request and top-level dispatch.

plain.headline: Saves work before risky steps
plain.oneLiner: Saves your session before each AI request and before risky tool calls.
plain.whatItDoes: Saves the session to durable storage just before the assistant asks the AI service for something, and just before a tool can affect the world outside. If that save fails, the step does not run.
plain.whyYoudCare: If the app crashes mid-task, this is what lets your work resume instead of losing the request or call under way.
useWhen: You use a storage plugin and want work to survive a crash.
You want a step that affects the outside world to wait for a successful save.
skipWhen: Nothing is saving your sessions, so there is nothing to save.
A specialised setup replaces this schedule with one of its own.
pros: A crash can be recovered from the stored requests, calls, replies, and results.
A failed save stops the risky step rather than letting it run.
It adds nothing to the assistant's instructions or its list of tools.
cons: It records that a call was sent, not that its effect outside actually happened.
A crash during a reply can lose the part that was still arriving.
A call saved without a result is marked unknown rather than retried.

name: dsh-session-format-v1-to-v2
catalogDescription: Frozen released-v1 Session codec and assistant-stream migration to v2
manifestDescription: Frozen released-v1 Session codec and assistant-stream migration to v2

readme.description: Frozen released-v1 Session reader and cardinality-changing migration that embeds Assistant streams in released v2 events.
readme.summary: `dsh-session-format-v1-to-v2` converts a released-v1 Session into the released-v2 event model through one stateful event stage. It consumes top-level `assistant/chunk` events, embeds their exact timed stream in the matching `assistant/message`, and records an `assistant/attempt` when a failed, retried, cancelled, or stream-error attempt reached settlement without a surface message. The edge densely remaps surviving events and every declared same-Session sequence reference, while the v2 codec stores one event per row and derives the inherited cut from a tagged `session/end-seed` marker.

name: dsh-session-persistence
catalogDescription: Abstract durable session persistence seam (ctx.sessionPersistence) for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Abstract durable session persistence seam (ctx.sessionPersistence) for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The durable session-storage seam for users and maintainers choosing a persistence backend, resuming sessions, or building a backend against the shared service contract.
readme.summary: This package lets applications persist and resume session event logs through a backend-independent API. Readers can create, open, inspect, list, append to, read, flush, and close stored sessions while preserving contiguous append-only history. A completed flush is the durability barrier; readers never receive torn tails or invalid records, and only one writer per session is allowed within a backend instance. Use the shipped [JSONL backend](../session-persistence-jsonl/README.md) for one compressed log per session, or implement another backend with the same observable guarantees.

name: dsh-session-persistence-jsonl
catalogDescription: JSONL durable session persistence backend for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: JSONL durable session persistence backend for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The shipped JSONL session-persistence backend for deployments and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging per-session durable logs with optional Zstandard compression.
readme.summary: `dsh-session-persistence-jsonl` stores each session in a current append-only JSONL log and retains immutable historical format generations — checksummed Zstandard frames by default, raw newline-delimited lines when compression is disabled. It serves the current logical `SessionEvent` stream through persistence handles, so format migration, compression, historical decoding, and crash recovery remain storage-internal details. Choose it when consumers need a per-session file on disk; the logs are readable as plain lines when `compression: 'none'` is selected. A root directory is the one required configuration; durability, lazy materialization, [supported historical-format migration](../session-format-catalog/README.md), and torn-tail crash recovery come with the backend.

plain.headline: Saves every session to a file on disk
plain.oneLiner: Keeps every session in its own log file on disk so nothing is lost.
plain.whatItDoes: Writes each session to its own log file on disk, appending as the conversation grows. If the app crashes, the saved log is what lets the session carry on from where it stopped.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is why your sessions still exist after you close the app or restart your computer.
useWhen: You want your conversations to survive a restart or a crash.
You want each session kept as one file you can find, back up, or read with other tools.
skipWhen: You never return to an old session and start fresh every time.
pros: Your history survives crashes and restarts.
Each session is a single file, easy to back up or inspect.
Turning compression off gives you a log you can read line by line.
cons: Nothing deletes old session files, so they accumulate until you remove them yourself.
Compressed logs cannot be read as plain lines without the app.
Only one writer can hold a session open at a time.
Older pre-release file layouts are not loaded; you must move them or use a separate folder.

name: dsh-session-projection
catalogDescription: Session-projection seam: the merge-extensible projection type table, the provider contract, and the ctx.sessionProjections registry serving whole current values of log-derived per-session state
manifestDescription: Session-projection seam: the merge-extensible projection type table, the provider contract, and the ctx.sessionProjections registry serving whole current values of log-derived per-session state

readme.description: The session-projection registry for developers serving whole current values of log-derived per-session state to client carriers, and for maintainers of the drive contract.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-session-projection` when clients need current per-session state—such as todos, goals, or conversation statistics—without replaying the raw event log. Domains define synchronous projections from committed session events, and clients receive complete, schema-validated JSON values through snapshots and change notifications. Snapshots identify the last event reflected by every returned value, so carriers can pair state with the matching history cut. Projection state can be checkpointed for faster cold reads, while host-only projections remain private to the host.

rationale:
Shared projection registry: subagent catalog identity (mode/label) folds
through its registered units, so the `list_agents` surface below fails
loud without it; web layers reuse this same mount for list rows.

plain.headline: Keeps live session state ready to show
plain.oneLiner: Internal service that keeps current session state ready for the interface.
plain.whatItDoes: Keeps the current state of a session, such as its to-do list, its goal, or its statistics, ready for the interface to display without replaying the whole conversation each time.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the plumbing that lets the interface show your to-do list, goal, or session statistics without re-reading the entire log.
useWhen: You are building a panel that must always show the current state of a session.
skipWhen: You only keep state on the machine running the app and no window ever displays it.
pros: A displayed value is current by construction, with no replay needed.
Values arrive with the point in history they reflect, so state and history line up.
State can be saved as a checkpoint so a cold start reads faster.
cons: Every update carries every visible value, with no way to ask for just one.
A value registered by any setup shows up in every session, so a missing value does not mean a missing feature.
Every event is checked against every value, which would need tuning if values became large.
State lives only in memory, so a restart rebuilds it by replaying the log.

name: dsh-session-projection-cache
catalogDescription: Persisted projection cache (ctx.sessionProjectionCache): durable per-session checkpoint records on the session_projcache storage domain (per-record layout), throttled write-behind, and the cached listing read
manifestDescription: Persisted projection cache (ctx.sessionProjectionCache): durable per-session checkpoint records on the session_projcache storage domain (per-record layout), throttled write-behind, and the cached listing read

readme.description: The persisted session-projection cache for deployments and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging durable checkpoints, zero-I/O list reads, and accelerated cold projection folds.
readme.summary: This package keeps durable per-session projection checkpoints so history lists, statistics, and goal snapshots can read cached values without loading each session log. Cold projection folds can resume after the checkpointed prefix, reducing restart work. The session log remains authoritative: a crash can leave a checkpoint stale, but never ahead of committed events, and incompatible records are ignored or backed up. Choose it for restarted sessions with frequent projection reads; skip it when projections are live-only or extra storage writes and unbounded checkpoint retention outweigh the saved work.

rationale:
Persisted projection cache: throttled write-behind over the
session_projcache domain (per-record layout — one version-stamped
checkpoint document per session), serving the session listing's
projection column.

plain.headline: Caches session state between restarts
plain.oneLiner: Stores session summaries on disk so lists and statistics load without full logs.
plain.whatItDoes: Stores checkpoints of the state derived from each session, so history lists, statistics, and goal snapshots can be shown without loading every saved log.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what lets history lists and statistics open quickly once you have many long sessions.
useWhen: You restart the app often and expect history lists and statistics to appear quickly.
You have many saved sessions and want their summaries shown without loading each one.
skipWhen: You only ever look at the session you are in right now.
You would rather not pay the extra disk writes for faster reads.
pros: History lists, statistics, and goal snapshots read stored values instead of full logs.
After a restart, rebuilding state resumes from the last checkpoint instead of the beginning.
The saved session log stays the authority, so a stale checkpoint can never be ahead of it.
cons: Stored checkpoints are never cleaned up, so pruning them is manual work.
The write timer is coarse: a slow trickle of changes still writes once per interval.
It never reads the session log itself, so a guaranteed fresh snapshot must be rebuilt elsewhere.

manifestDescription: Concrete ctx.sessionQuery backend with SQLite FTS5 search

readme.description: The SQLite FTS5 full-text search backend for session history, for deployments and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging full-text search over the query service.
readme.summary: Use this package to add ranked SQLite FTS5 search across session history, either across sessions or within one session, with cursor pagination. It indexes live and persisted history in a separate derived database, so searches reflect current state without modifying the session-persistence store. Exact reads, filters, and traces remain available through the same query API. Search is opt-in in shipped compositions; configure `openAt` to open the index at startup, on first search, or never. Results match tokens and phrases rather than arbitrary substrings, and each index path has a single process owner.

headings.text: When to defer or disable search

rationale:
Full-text session search is opt-in. `openAt: never` keeps
ctx.sessionQuery mounted — exact reads, titles, and lineage traces
(session export, subagent-fork Workspace inheritance) stay available —
while search calls fail with SESSION_QUERY_SEARCH_DISABLED and SQLite is
never opened; the Web sidebar search matches titles and workspace names
only. Deployments enabling content search override `openAt` to
`first-search` or `startup` in a later patch layer (profile
cordis.patch.yml or a --patch overlay), typically with a durable `path`.

Full-text session search is opt-in (the base row's `openAt: never`). This
restatement keeps the Web values on one ephemeral in-memory index; a
deployment enabling content search overrides `openAt` to `first-search` in a
later patch layer, which defers the node:sqlite import and in-memory handle
to the first search so Node 22 startup stays quiet.

plain.headline: Search the words inside past sessions
plain.oneLiner: Adds ranked search over session history; content search is off until you turn it on.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds ranked full-text search across your session history, within one session or across all of them, with paging. In this build content search is switched off: exact lookups, titles, and lineage still work.
plain.whyYoudCare: Content search is off unless someone turns it on, so this decides whether you can find old conversations by what was said.
useWhen: You want to find an old session by words that appeared inside it.
You are willing to change one setting to switch content search on.
skipWhen: You only need exact lookups, titles, or tracing where a session came from.
You do not want a second searchable copy of your conversations on disk.
pros: Finds sessions by words and phrases across your whole history.
Results come back ranked, and you can page through them.
Searching uses a separate copy, so your saved sessions are not modified.
cons: Content search is off in this build and has to be switched on by configuration.
It matches whole words and phrases, not fragments inside a word.
A search blocks the app while it runs and cannot be interrupted once started.
It does no access checking of its own, so anything that can query it sees every session.

name: dsh-session-reference
catalogDescription: Cross-session snapshot references and durable untrusted model context (ctx.sessionReferenceResolver)
manifestDescription: Cross-session snapshot references and durable untrusted model context (ctx.sessionReferenceResolver)

readme.description: Cross-session snapshot references and durable untrusted model context, for users and maintainers enabling or debugging ctx.sessionReferenceResolver.
readme.summary: `dsh-session-reference` lets a conversation reference other sessions: a host turns a `@label` mention into a canonical URI, and the service prepares a bounded, read-only snapshot of each referenced session as durable, untrusted background context for the model. Candidate discovery ranks other sessions by working-directory affinity and labels them with their latest titles. Snapshots are immutable after capture and carry a fixed warning that forbids following instructions, permission claims, or tool requests inside them. It is an opt-in service for hosts that support cross-session mentions; it consumes `ctx.sessionQuery` and needs no SQLite FTS.

plain.headline: Mention one session inside another
plain.oneLiner: Lets you @mention another session and hand the model a short, frozen snapshot of it.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets you point at another session with an @mention and gives the model a short, read-only snapshot of it. Every snapshot carries a warning that it must not be treated as instructions.
plain.whyYoudCare: It lets you reuse the context of another session without copying and pasting text between them.
useWhen: You want the assistant to use what was settled in a different session.
You are continuing work whose background lives in another conversation.
skipWhen: Your sessions have nothing to do with each other.
You would rather paste the few relevant lines yourself.
pros: You can bring another session's context in without copying text.
Candidate sessions are ranked by shared working folder and shown by their titles.
Each snapshot is frozen at capture time and marked as untrusted background.
cons: Only text crosses over; images and other non-text content are left behind.
It looks at titles, not message bodies, so you cannot find a session by what was said inside it.
A reference is a one-off snapshot: there is no live link, and later changes to the source do not appear.
Sessions saved before the projection cache was in place only get a title back once you open them.

name: dsh-session-stats

useWhen: You watch how many turns and steps a session takes.
You want timing figures that stay the same after a reload.

You can see model time and time to the first word of the reply, not just totals.
The figures survive paging and history reduction.

The numbers cover the whole session, including parts that were later trimmed away.

name: dsh-session-telemetry

readme.description: Session-telemetry capture seam for deployments and backend authors choosing a reporting backend, mounting redaction rules, or implementing the backend contract.
readme.summary: Session telemetry lets deployments send ordered copies of session activity for reporting while preserving the canonical session log. Deployments choose one reporting backend and can redact each outbound copy before delivery; without redaction rules, captured data leaves the process unchanged. The handoff is non-blocking, so reporting does not delay session processing. Delivery is best effort, and queued records may be lost if the process crashes.

plain.headline: Sends copies of session activity out
plain.oneLiner: Internal helper copying session activity to a reporting destination. Nothing to configure.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that copies session activity to a reporting destination chosen by whoever runs the deployment, without changing the saved session. There is nothing here for you to configure.

name: dsh-session-telemetry-otel
catalogDescription: Feedback-authorized Session logs over byte-bounded OpenTelemetry HTTP requests
manifestDescription: Feedback-authorized Session logs over byte-bounded OpenTelemetry HTTP requests

readme.description: OpenTelemetry session-telemetry backend for deployments choosing a mode, configuring the exporter, or tracing what leaves the machine.
readme.summary:
The adapter injects `otel`; the [shared OTel plugin](../../telemetry/otel/README.md) creates its independent Session-log channel. Authorization, redaction, identity, scope version, configuration, and the shutdown deadline remain owned here.

`dsh-session-telemetry-otel` exports session records through the OTel JS SDK only after new explicit feedback, for all users and providers, including `deepseek-official`. `FEEDBACK_ONLY` releases the canonical prefix through that feedback, including context; later records wait for the next explicit feedback. `DISABLED` constructs no transport. Scheduled batching can finish an authorized upload without another user interaction or model call. Deployments own their redaction rules.

rationale:
OTel releases a Session-log prefix only after explicit user feedback,
regardless of model provider. Ordinary activity never triggers capture.
DSH_TELEMETRY_OTLP_URL overrides the production endpoint. A non-empty
DSH_TELEMETRY_DISABLED — any value, including '0'/'false' — opts the
process out (the launchers patch the row disabled; config cannot disable
a row). Exports carry the harness home's anonymous user id ($DSH_HOME/.anonymous-user-id,
random UUID; delete the file to reset the identity) as the Resource's
user.id. Byte-bounded batching may turn an authorized prefix into
several HTTP requests. Requests run serially; each has its own 1s
transport timeout and 1.5s watchdog. A watchdog does not release the
active request slot. The outer 3s shutdown deadline stops queued sends;
large prefixes or an unsettled transport may leave records unsent.
Every CLI exit path drains by disposing the root on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

plain.headline: Sends session logs only after feedback
plain.oneLiner: Uploads session records only after you give feedback, and can be switched off.
plain.whatItDoes: Sends a copy of a session's records to a collection service, but only after you give explicit feedback. With the default mode, ordinary activity never triggers a send.
plain.whyYoudCare: It decides whether records of your sessions ever leave your machine, and you can switch it off with one environment setting.
useWhen: You want your feedback about a session to arrive together with the records that explain it.
You run a deployment and want session records sent to your own collection service.
skipWhen: You do not want session records leaving your machine at all.
You never give feedback on sessions.
pros: Nothing is sent until you explicitly give feedback.
You can point it at your own collection address instead of the default one.
One environment setting opts your machine out completely, whatever the value.
cons: After a restart, a new feedback submission can repeat records already sent, and the receiver must sort out duplicates.
There is no guaranteed delivery, no automatic retry, and no confirmation that the collector accepted it.
Feedback given while this was switched off is not replayed when it returns.
Withdrawing feedback sends a deletion notice, not proof that remote copies were erased.
Rules about what gets blanked out before sending are left to whoever runs the deployment.

name: dsh-session-title
catalogDescription: Log-backed session title service and provider registry for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Log-backed session title service and provider registry for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: Log-backed session titles for users and maintainers choosing a title source, configuring the service, or debugging title state.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-session-title` to give each session a client-visible title from the first eligible human message, an optional asynchronous generator, or an explicit user rename. Accepted titles persist through replay, resume, and paging but never enter model input. Automatic generation never delays the main agent response, and newer title requests supersede older work. Choose the package when clients need durable titles with configurable length limits and a deliberate `refresh()` path for regenerating them.

plain.headline: Gives every session a readable name
plain.oneLiner: Gives each session a short title that is kept but never sent to the model.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives each session a short title taken from your first eligible message, from a generator, or from a rename you type. Titles survive replay, resume, and paging, and are never sent to the model.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the reason your sessions have names you can recognise instead of numbers.
useWhen: You want to tell your sessions apart in a list.
You renamed a session and want that name kept.
You asked for a title to be generated again.
skipWhen: You never look back at sessions you have finished.
pros: Sessions get readable names without you typing anything.
A name you set by hand is kept through replays and resumes.
Generating a name never delays the main answer.
Titles never reach the model, so they cost no input.
cons: It cannot delete or search titles, and it does not index them for listing.
Going back to automatic titles after unpinning only happens when you ask for a refresh.
Only one title strategy can be active at a time.

name: dsh-session-title-first-prompt-llm
catalogDescription: First-message LLM provider plugin for DeepSeek Harness session titles
manifestDescription: First-message LLM provider plugin for DeepSeek Harness session titles

readme.description: First-message LLM session-title provider for users and maintainers choosing a title strategy or debugging automatic title generation.
readme.summary: `dsh-session-title-first-prompt-llm` summarizes the first eligible human message through `ctx.llm` as an optional `ctx.sessionTitle` provider. It registers the `first-prompt` cadence, runs automatically only when a fresh non-fork session first creates its fallback, and attributes the result to that message's exact seq. An automatic failure retains the fallback and is retried only through `ctx.sessionTitle.refresh()`. It uses the complete required shared LLM configuration from `dsh-session-title-llm`, so route, prompt, budget, and cancellation behavior cannot drift. Automatic behavior and configuration come first; the implementation is a thin registration over the shared policy.

plain.headline: Names a session from its first message
plain.oneLiner: Uses the model to turn your first message into a short session title.
plain.whatItDoes: Asks the model to summarise your first message into a short session title. It runs by itself only for a brand-new session, and a failure leaves the plain automatic title in place.
plain.whyYoudCare: It turns your opening message into a tidy session name instead of a clipped copy of your own words.
useWhen: You want titles that read like summaries rather than cut-off first lines.
You are starting fresh sessions that will run for a while.
skipWhen: You prefer titles taken straight from your own words.
Most of your work happens in sessions copied from another session.
pros: Titles read like a summary of what the session is about.
If generation fails, the plain fallback title stays and nothing breaks.
One shared configuration sets routing, wording, size limits, and cancellation.
cons: A long session can outgrow a title drawn from its first message alone.
Sessions copied from another session keep the inherited title and are never renamed automatically.
After a failure, a new title is only attempted when you explicitly ask for a refresh.

name: dsh-session-title-llm

manifestDescription: Shared LLM generation policy for DeepSeek Harness session-title providers

readme.summary: `dsh-session-title-llm` generates concise session titles from selected human messages with a consistent model request policy. Callers choose which messages contribute to each revision and may either supply a provider and model route together or use the route recorded for the current session. Required limits cap the framed input, generated output, and end-to-end duration, while caller cancellation remains effective throughout streaming. Invalid, empty, late, tool-call, or otherwise non-text results are rejected before they can replace a title.

plain.headline: Names sessions with a short title

plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that asks the AI service for a short title based on chosen messages. Title add-ons built on it decide when, and there is nothing here for you to configure.

name: dsh-session-turn-outline

readme.description: Whole-log turn outline for clients and maintainers composing or debugging the turnOutline projection unit behind full-session turn navigation.
readme.summary: This package gives history clients a whole-session outline of every started turn, including bounded prompt and settled-response previews. Clients can navigate turns that are not yet loaded and page backward from the exact event sequence needed to load a selected turn. It fits assemblies that provide session projections; elsewhere, clients continue using loaded-window navigation. Previews exclude injected context and tool results, and a response appears only after its turn settles.

rationale:
Whole-log turn outline for the chat turn rail (the turnOutline
projection key): every turn stays navigable before its events page in.

plain.headline: Outlines every turn in a session
plain.oneLiner: Lists every turn with short previews so you can jump around a long session.
plain.whatItDoes: Builds a compact outline of every turn in a session, with short previews of the prompt and the finished reply. It lets the interface reach turns whose full contents are not loaded.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what lets you jump around a long conversation without waiting for the whole thing to load.
useWhen: You work in long sessions and want to jump between turns.
You page backward to a particular earlier turn.
skipWhen: Your sessions are short enough to load all at once.
pros: Every turn stays reachable before its contents are loaded.
Previews leave out injected background and tool output, so they stay readable.
You can page backward from the exact point a chosen turn begins.
cons: The outline grows with the session, so a very long session makes it large.
An answer only gets a preview once its turn has finished.
Turns with no text, such as images or commands only, are numbered but not described.

name: dsh-settings

manifestDescription: Abstract user-settings seam (ctx.settings) for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: Inspect and edit live plugin configuration through Config-derived forms.
readme.summary: Edit fields that plugins declare with `.volatile()` and inspect their effective values. Forms identify each plugin by its profile entry id, preserve secret values, and refuse stale writes. Changes persist through the active profile’s Cordis patch.

plain.headline: Edit plugin settings from a form
plain.oneLiner: Lets you edit plugin settings in a form and save them to the profile you are running.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives you a form for settings that plugins declare, so you can change a value and see which one is really in effect. It preserves secret values and refuses a save made from an out-of-date form.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how a setting you change sticks to the profile you are running, without editing configuration files by hand.
useWhen: You want to change an option a plugin offers without editing a configuration file.
You need to see which value is really in effect after several layers of settings.
skipWhen: You are happy editing the harness configuration files yourself.
The setting you want is supplied by a nested include, which these forms do not cover.
pros: Changes are saved through the profile you are running, so they survive a restart
Secret values are kept as secrets rather than shown or wiped
A save made from a stale form is refused instead of overwriting a newer value
cons: Settings supplied by a nested include keep their own configuration and are not editable through the active profile's form
A field-level reset restores the inherited value, but it cannot delete a value set by a lower layer
Removing an item from a list removes that item rather than restoring an earlier one

name: dsh-shell
catalogDescription: Abstract bash executor seam (ctx.shell) for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Abstract bash executor seam (ctx.shell) for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The shell executor seam for developers and maintainers choosing, composing, or implementing command execution over ctx.shell.
readme.summary: Use `ctx.shell` to run shell commands with bounded output or keep them running as background work. One execution handle supports foreground results and background reads. A profile can select local or sandboxed Bash or PowerShell execution without changing callers. Resolve requests before execution to make the working directory, timeout, and output limits explicit. Command exits, timeouts, and caller aborts return results; only infrastructure failures reject, while the `bash` and `pwsh` tools own model-visible rendering and sandbox guidance.

plain.headline: Runs shell commands for other parts
plain.oneLiner: Internal helper for running shell commands. Nothing for you to configure.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that lets other parts of the harness run shell commands, read their output, and keep long work going in the background. There is nothing here for you to configure.

name: dsh-shell-env
catalogDescription: Tool-independent managed DSH_* shell environment registry
manifestDescription: Tool-independent managed DSH_* shell environment registry

readme.description: The managed DSH_* shell environment for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or extending the environment every model shell call runs with.
readme.summary: `dsh-shell-env` provides the trusted `DSH_*` environment that every model shell call — bash or pwsh — runs with: built-in facts such as `DSH_HOME`, `DSH_SHELL=1`, the agent's `DSH_SESSION_ID`, and the launched profile's `DSH_PROFILE` and `DSH_PROFILE_DIR`. Plugin authors can register their own facts with declared keys, collected per execution and disposed with their plugin; duplicate ownership or undeclared runtime keys fail loudly instead of silently overwriting. The registry changes nothing else the model sees — the shell tools own their own schemas and prompts. Choose it in any composition that mounts a model shell tool; configuration only picks the Harness home directory.

plain.headline: Trusted settings for shell commands
plain.oneLiner: Gives every shell command a trusted, consistent set of harness values.
plain.whatItDoes: Sets the small set of named values that every command the assistant runs in a shell receives, such as the harness home folder, the session id, and the profile in use. Other plugins can add their own values to the same list.
plain.whyYoudCare: It makes the commands the assistant runs behave the same way every time instead of inheriting whatever your shell happened to have set.
useWhen: You want commands run for you to see the harness home folder and the current session id.
You combine plugins that need to advertise values to shell commands.
skipWhen: Your sessions never run shell commands.
You only care about the assistant reading and editing files.
pros: Every shell call gets a freshly built, trusted set of values instead of an inherited one
Two plugins cannot quietly claim the same name, because a clash fails loudly
Values added by a plugin are cleaned up when that plugin goes away
cons: The list of values it can report covers only the ones plugins add, not its own built-in values
It changes nothing else a shell command sees, such as the options and instructions of the shell tools themselves

name: dsh-skill

manifestDescription: Agent skill provider registry for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The skill provider registry for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging how skills from any source are merged, resolved, and loaded.
readme.summary: Use this package to give agents and users one catalog of reusable, task-specific instructions collected from local directories, embedded plugin data, or remote services. It resolves duplicate names predictably, validates entries, tolerates unavailable sources without discarding usable results, and loads the selected skill's full instructions on demand. Mount it when a composition needs skills from multiple or non-filesystem sources; pair it with `dsh-skill-filesystem` for local discovery and `dsh-tool-skill` for model access, because it includes no skill content itself.

plain.headline: One catalog of ready-made instructions
plain.oneLiner: Keeps one catalog of prepared instructions the assistant can choose from.
plain.whatItDoes: Collects reusable, task-specific instructions from several places into one catalog an assistant can browse, and loads the full instructions of the one it picks only when they are needed. It supplies the catalog, not the instructions themselves.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how the assistant finds the right written instructions for a job instead of making up an approach.
useWhen: Your instructions come from more than one place, or from somewhere other than your own disk.
You want a single list of what is available rather than several separate ones.
skipWhen: Your sessions never load prepared instructions.
Everything is short enough that the assistant does not need written procedures.
pros: One list shows everything available, whatever its source
Entries with the same name are resolved the same way every time
A source that is unavailable does not discard results from the sources that work
Only the chosen instructions are loaded in full
cons: It cannot notice on its own that a remote source changed, so each source has to report that itself
Sources are checked one after another, so one slow source delays all the ones after it
When two entries share a name the first wins, and there is no way to see what was hidden
It keeps no fallback copy and no report about a source that failed
Stopping a lookup stops your wait, but cannot stop work a source keeps doing on its own

name: dsh-skill-badge

manifestDescription: Bundled dsh badge skill provider for DeepSeek Harness

The provider has no configuration, and the shipped CLI composition includes the plugin disabled, so deployments enable it explicitly. The skill ships both Markdown snippets and a packaged PNG for systems that cannot reliably import remote images.

plain.headline: Add the official dsh badge
plain.oneLiner: Ships the official dsh badge instructions for documents and code reviews.
plain.whatItDoes: Offers the assistant one built-in set of instructions for adding the official dsh attribution badge to documents, code reviews, and other content you produce. It includes ready-made markup and an image file for places that cannot fetch images from the web.

You would rather have the badge text supplied than write it yourself.

You need a badge other than the official one.

An image file is included for systems that cannot fetch images from the web
cons: It offers exactly one badge, with no way to change it at run time

name: dsh-skill-filesystem
catalogDescription: Local filesystem skill provider for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Local filesystem skill provider for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The local filesystem skill provider for users and maintainers authoring local skills or configuring how project, custom, and user skill roots are discovered and watched.
readme.summary: Agents can use local skills from the repository, a custom directory, or the user's agent configuration: author a skill as a directory bundle with a `SKILL.md` or a flat `<name>.md` file under any scanned root, and it appears in the session catalog. The provider discovers the project, custom, and user roots, parses each skill's YAML frontmatter, and watches the directories, so new, renamed, or deleted skills reach agents without a restart. Choose it when skills live on disk — the registry (`dsh-skill`) accepts any provider, and another provider can supply skills from elsewhere.

rationale:
The `skill` REGISTRY stays in the host plane. It is host+per-scope layered
(the tools-registry shape): deployment-level providers — repository plugins,
a host skill-filesystem row — register into its global layer, while a preset's
`skill-filesystem` registers into that preset's layer, and each agent reads the
merged catalog its scope chain selects. Only the per-agent rows move behind
presets: the base host `skill-filesystem` row is disabled here (presets own local
discovery), and `tool-skill` is what a preset mounts to give its agent the
catalog and loader at all.

plain.headline: Use instruction files kept on disk
plain.oneLiner: Watches folders of instruction files so the assistant can use the ones you write.
plain.whatItDoes: Finds instruction sets on disk, in your project, a folder you pick, or your personal agent setup, and updates the list as files change. It reads a folder holding a SKILL.md file and a single named file.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what makes instruction files you write on disk show up for the assistant without restarting anything.
useWhen: You keep your own sets of instructions in files on disk and want the assistant to use them.
You edit those files during a session and expect the change to take effect.
skipWhen: You never write instruction files yourself.
Your instructions arrive from a remote service or from inside a plugin.
pros: New, renamed, and deleted instruction files are noticed without a restart
It can read from your project, a folder you choose, and your personal setup
A problem reading the files leaves the last good list in place rather than emptying it
cons: Only one level of folders is searched, so deeper trees and package files are ignored
Your project is found by the nearest folder containing a .git marker, with no other way to choose it
A broken instruction file disappears with a warning, and the assistant cannot tell a missing set from a broken one
Changing a file after it was loaded affects later uses but does not correct results already produced
The base copy of this provider is switched off, so a setup that does not add its own will not see local instructions

plain.headline: Word, Excel and PowerPoint workflows

plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant prepared instructions for making and editing Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files. It also runs structural checks, and can render pages when an appropriate renderer is installed.

Pages or worksheet ranges can be rendered so you can see what a file looks like

name: dsh-spill
catalogDescription: Abstract spill storage seam (ctx.spillStore) for the DeepSeek Harness — save oversized tool text and return a retrieval locator
manifestDescription: Abstract spill storage seam (ctx.spillStore) for the DeepSeek Harness — save oversized tool text and return a retrieval locator

readme.description: The spill storage service: save oversized tool text or captured session references and return a retrievable locator.
readme.summary: `dsh-spill` lets plugins and tools save oversized text through the public `ctx.spillStore` API and receive an opaque locator, exact byte count, and retrieval guidance. Configure `dsh-spill-local` for local persistence, and add `dsh-spill-policy` when oversized tool results should become bounded previews. plain.headline: Stores oversized tool output
plain.oneLiner: Internal helper that parks oversized tool text for later. Nothing to configure.

name: dsh-spill-local

manifestDescription: Local-filesystem implementation of the DeepSeek Harness spill storage seam (private session-scoped files)

readme.description: The local filesystem spill backend: how spilled text is saved to private session-scoped files and retrieved with read or grep.
readme.summary: `dsh-spill-local` saves a caller's oversized text to a private, session-scoped file on the host filesystem and returns that file's path as the locator, with retrieval guidance telling the model to read or grep it. Files are private to the current user, names are unpredictable, and each session's files group under a stable directory, so a shared root cannot leak output or be redirected by a planted symlink. Configuration selects the root and the startup-cleanup retention period; previews and spill decisions live in other packages.

plain.headline: Keep huge outputs in a private file
plain.oneLiner: Saves oversized command output to a private file and passes back the path.
plain.whatItDoes: When a command produces far more text than is worth showing, this saves the whole result to a private file and hands back a path so it can be read or searched later. The files are private to your user account and their names are hard to guess.
plain.whyYoudCare: Long results are kept instead of being cut off, without filling the conversation with text you will never read.
useWhen: A command prints far more than you or the assistant need to see at once.
You want the full result kept somewhere you can search later in the session.
skipWhen: You work somewhere that does not allow temporary copies of output.
Your assistant runs on a different machine from the files it works with.
pros: Long results stay available instead of being truncated
Saved files are private to your user account
Unpredictable names make the stored output hard to reach by accident
Each session's files group under one stable folder
Old files are removed on a retention period you set
cons: Cleanup runs once when the plugin starts, so files that age out during a long run are only removed at the next start
The path it hands back only helps something that can read the same machine's files

name: dsh-spill-policy
catalogDescription: Token-budgeted tool-result retention with recoverable text and image paths
manifestDescription: Token-budgeted tool-result retention with recoverable text and image paths

readme.description: Tool-result retention with a shared text/image token budget and readable recovery files.
readme.summary: Keep oversized text and image results within a shared estimated token budget. The model receives ordered head/tail content and a path to the complete result. Images remain in attachment storage; the result file records their readable paths. Omitting `maxInlineTokens` disables retention, and recovery failures leave the original content visible.

plain.headline: Trim huge results, keep a way back
plain.oneLiner: Limits how much of a long result enters the conversation, keeping the rest on disk.
plain.whatItDoes: Puts a ceiling on how much of an oversized result stays in the conversation. The assistant sees the beginning and the end plus a pointer to the complete result on disk, and images stay in their own store with their readable paths recorded.
plain.whyYoudCare: It stops one chatty command from crowding out the rest of the conversation and making the session slower and costlier.
useWhen: Long command output or large images keep crowding out the rest of a session.
You want the complete result available even when only part of it is shown.

cons: Text is priced by character count and structure, not an exact length.
Every measurement copies the current state, so even a small check costs time.
Stored usage figures are reused only when the request is identical.
A rewritten system prompt is not repriced until the next real call.

name: dsh-tool-ask-user

plain.headline: Lets the assistant ask you a question
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant ask you to confirm, choose, or supply a missing detail.

The assistant needs a detail only you know.

You cannot risk a question going missing halfway.

With a time limit it can carry on working while the question waits.

name: dsh-tool-bash

readme.description: The model-facing bash tool for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging one-shot command execution, background jobs, and sandbox escalation.
readme.summary: `dsh-tool-bash` runs Bash commands and returns stdout, stderr, and exit markers. Each call uses a fresh shell; cwd, variables, and functions do not persist. With a job registry composed, every command is a job from its start: `run_in_background` returns the id at once, a foreground command that outlives its timeout returns the same id, and `job_output`/`job_kill` collect and stop it. Commands receive the managed `DSH_*` environment; sandbox denials can be retried once with wider `sandbox_permissions`, a `justification`, and user approval. Nonzero exits are results for the agent to interpret. Mount an executor such as `dsh-bash-local` or `dsh-bash-sandbox` with `dsh-shell-env`.

headings.text: Running long commands in the background

plain.headline: Runs commands on your computer
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant run command-line programs and read their output.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant the ability to run command-line programs on your machine and read back what they printed, including whether they succeeded. Each command starts in a fresh shell.

useWhen: A task needs a command-line tool or a build step.
You want a long command to keep running while you do other things.
skipWhen: You only want the assistant to read and write files.
You are not willing to let it run commands on your machine.
pros: You see the output, the errors, and whether the command succeeded
Commands can run in the background while the assistant gets on with something else
If the safety boundary around a command blocks it, it can ask you once for wider access
cons: It is switched off in this build.
Each command starts fresh, so a change of folder or a setting does not carry over.
Background work has no time limit; something has to stop it explicitly.
Output ending with a line that looks like an exit marker can be mislabelled when you replay the session.
It is left out of the shared time limits and keeps its own.

headings.text: What the agent can rely on

plain.headline: A command shell that remembers
plain.oneLiner: Runs commands in a shell that keeps its folder, settings, and background work.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant a command shell that remembers where it is, what it set, and what it started, so a run of commands can build on each other. Each assistant gets its own shell and commands run one at a time.
plain.whyYoudCare: Some work only makes sense as a run of commands in the same shell, and the ordinary command tool forgets everything between calls.
useWhen: You are working through commands that build on each other.
You need a started tool to stay alive across steps.

name: dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy

headings.text: How a deadline is armed and mapped

plain.headline: Puts a time limit on slow tool calls
plain.oneLiner: Ends a slow tool call with a clear timeout message when the tool agrees to stop.
plain.whatItDoes: Asks a tool to stop when it runs past the limit set for it, then reports to the assistant that the call timed out instead of leaving it waiting. Calls that finish in time are untouched.
plain.whyYoudCare: Without a limit, one stuck step can leave a session hanging with no explanation.
useWhen: A step seems to be hanging with no answer.
You are setting time limits on tools that honour them.
skipWhen: You need a tool stopped by force.
You expect one shared limit to cover every tool.
pros: A slow call ends with a clear message instead of silence
Tools that finish within their limit behave exactly as before
cons: It can only ask a tool to stop; a tool that ignores the request keeps running and keeps you waiting.

name: dsh-tool-cordis

plain.headline: Look up how the app is built

It only reads; it cannot change anything or run code for you

name: dsh-tool-fs
