readme.description: The model-facing read, read_image, write, and edit tools for users and maintainers composing or debugging filesystem access for agents.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-tool-fs` to let a model read UTF-8 files with line numbers, read supported images, create or atomically replace files, and apply targeted literal edits. plain.headline: Read, write, and edit your files
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant read, create, and make careful edits to your files.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets the assistant read text files with line numbers, look at images, create or replace files, and make small exact edits to text. Results are capped, and failures come back with a clear code and a way to recover.

useWhen: You want the assistant to change a file on disk.
You want it to read a file or an image you point at.
skipWhen: You only want searching and listing, not reading or writing.
You are not comfortable with the assistant changing files.
pros: Edits are small and exact instead of rewriting a whole file
Reads come back with line numbers, which makes later edits precise
Failures explain themselves and say how to recover
cons: It is switched off in this build.
It reads text only; images use a separate tool, and PDFs, sound, and video are not supported.
There is no built-in way to list a folder; a separate package handles searching.
Files are protected from being overwritten before they are read only if you add the extra guard package.
An image saved under the wrong file extension is refused instead of being detected.

name: dsh-tool-fs-search

Configurable caps bound inline output; with an optional spill store, capped results remain fully recoverable. Choose the sibling `dsh-tool-fs` package for reading, writing, or editing files.

plain.headline: Find files and search inside them
plain.oneLiner: Finds files by name and searches their contents, with nothing to install.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant two ways to explore a folder: find files by name pattern, and search inside files for text. Paths come back relative to where you are working, with nothing extra to install.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how the assistant finds the right file in a large project without you listing every path yourself.
useWhen: You ask about something in a large folder or a codebase.
You want to know where a word or phrase appears.
skipWhen: Your files live on a remote or virtual drive.
You need files outside the workspace you are working in.
pros: Hidden files are included and version-control clutter is left out
Results list the most recently changed files first
It needs nothing installed on your machine to work
cons: It is switched off in this build.
Found paths can only be opened afterwards when the search root and the file root are the same place.
Long results stop at a cap; keeping everything needs an optional storage add-on.

When oversized results are sampled, the balancing only reaches top-level folders, so one busy deep folder can still dominate.

name: dsh-tool-goal
catalogDescription: Model-facing same-session goal tools with execution-time authority checks
manifestDescription: Model-facing same-session goal tools with execution-time authority checks

readme.description: The model-facing goal tools for users and maintainers choosing, composing, or debugging get_goal, create_goal, and update_goal.
readme.summary: `dsh-tool-goal` lets a model read persisted goals and infer and create a long-running goal from a direct human request. Creating, editing, pausing, or resuming requires that direct request in a top-level agent turn; completing or blocking also works in an autonomous goal round. Updates require the exact goal id and revision returned by a prior read. `resume` rearms active-but-disarmed or blocked goals, while users resume durable paused goals through Web or `/goal resume`. Autonomous blocking requires the same condition for a configurable threshold of three consecutive rounds by default.

rationale:
Persisted same-session goals reach the model and the slash menu here; the
domain, driver, and `/goal` command are above.

plain.headline: Keeps a long goal on track
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant track a long goal and pause, resume, finish, or block it.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets the assistant read the goal saved for this session and start one when you ask for it directly. It can pause, resume, finish, or mark a goal blocked, and it checks the exact version it last read before changing anything.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how a long piece of work is tracked as one goal rather than a single answer.
useWhen: You ask for something that will take many steps.
You want to pause or resume a long piece of work.
skipWhen: Your request is a single quick answer.
pros: Only a direct request from you can start, pause, or change a goal
It checks the exact version it last read, so two updates cannot clash
Finishing or blocking also works during unattended rounds
cons: It is switched off in this build.
Judging whether your request is substantial enough to be a goal is left to the assistant.
Treating an obstacle as the same one again is also judgement; the app only counts rounds.
The tools change state only; they do not schedule anything or show you a page by themselves.
Unattended finish or block does nothing unless a continuation driver is also running.

name: dsh-tool-jobs
catalogDescription: Model-facing background job control tools (job_output, job_list, job_kill) over the ctx.jobs registry
manifestDescription: Model-facing background job control tools (job_output, job_list, job_kill) over the ctx.jobs registry

readme.description: The model-facing background-job controls for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging job_output, job_list, job_kill, and completion notices.
readme.summary: Use `dsh-tool-jobs` to inspect and control background commands, PTY work, and subagents through `job_output`, `job_list`, and `job_kill`. Reads can wait within a configured timeout, list results identify each job's kind and status, and cancellation settles only after the work stops. When owned work finishes, the agent receives an in-session notice: busy agents receive it in their next step, while idle agents are woken by a follow-up turn. Configuration controls wait limits, completion delivery, and an optional cap on consecutive wakeups. Stream output is consumed by one reader, and pending notices do not survive owner disposal.

rationale:
The background-job REGISTRY stays on the host plane; only the model-facing
`job_*` controls move. Its producers — `tool-bash` here, `tool-terminal` and a
non-continuable `tool-subagent` elsewhere — are preset rows that resolve it
with `ctx.get`, and an entry-local realm around the registry is invisible to
every sibling row outside that realm, so `run_in_background` answered
"background jobs unavailable" while the controls sat in the catalog. That is
the `goals` criterion read from inside the preset: a Service a row outside its
realm READS belongs to the plane both can see. The registry is keyed by owning
agent, so one host instance serves every session exactly as before presets.

plain.headline: Watch and stop background work
plain.oneLiner: Check on, wait for, and stop background work the assistant started.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant three controls over background work: read what a job has produced, list what is running, and stop it. It also tells the assistant when work it started has finished.
plain.whyYoudCare: Long commands and helper assistants can keep working while the conversation continues, and this is how they are watched and stopped.
useWhen: You have a long command that should keep running.
You want to check on or cancel background work.
skipWhen: Everything you ask for finishes in one step.
pros: A read can wait a set time for news instead of checking constantly
Stopping a job reports success only once the work has actually stopped
The assistant is told when its background work finishes, even while it is busy
cons: It is switched off in this build.
A job that settles at an awkward moment can leave its notice stranded.
When a limit on consecutive wake-ups is set, only your own message refills it, and nothing on screen shows a notice is waiting.
A waiting notice is lost if the assistant is shut down first.
Only one reader can follow a job's output, so a second viewer gets nothing.

name: dsh-tool-present
catalogDescription: Explicit workspace file delivery declarations for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Explicit workspace file delivery declarations for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: Declare accessible files as deliverables with present; configuration, Session ownership, and source-file opening.
readme.summary: Use `present` to declare final files accessible through the Session filesystem, including files created through shell commands. Users open the current source files in their default application. The tool records paths and optional descriptions without copying file contents.

plain.headline: Hand finished files to you
plain.oneLiner: Marks the files the assistant finished so you can open them in one click.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets the assistant flag the files it finished making, so you get a card for each one and can open it in your usual application. It records the path and your note, and leaves the file itself where it is.
plain.whyYoudCare: It turns a pile of files the assistant touched into a short list you can open directly, instead of hunting through folders.
useWhen: You asked for a document, spreadsheet or slide deck and want a link to it.
You want to know exactly which files this session produced.
skipWhen: You are happy to find the output files yourself in your workspace.
pros: You get a clear list of what was produced, not just a chat reply
Your files are never copied or moved just to be shown to you
Opening an entry uses the current file in your usual application
cons: A file can be changed or replaced between the listing and the moment your application opens it.
If you later delete or move the file, the saved entry can no longer open it.
Exported session archives keep the entries but not the file contents.

name: dsh-tool-pwsh
catalogDescription: Model-facing pwsh tool over the bash executor seam
manifestDescription: Model-facing pwsh tool over the bash executor seam

readme.description: The model-facing pwsh tool for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging one-shot PowerShell execution, background jobs, and sandbox escalation on Windows.
readme.summary: `dsh-tool-pwsh` lets the agent run PowerShell commands through a mounted shell executor. Each call uses a fresh process; with a job registry composed every command is a job from the moment it starts, so `run_in_background` returns the id at once and a foreground command that outlives its timeout returns the same id, with observable output. Commands use native Windows paths and `$env:NAME` variables without dialect translation. Calls receive the managed `DSH_*` environment, and sandboxed execution enforces Windows language-mode and named-pipe requirements. Mount it with a PowerShell executor such as `dsh-pwsh-local` and the `dsh-shell-env` plugin.

plain.headline: Run PowerShell commands
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant run PowerShell commands, including in the background.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant a way to run PowerShell commands on your machine, one fresh process per command. Commands use normal Windows paths and environment variables, and long ones can run in the background.
plain.whyYoudCare: On Windows this is how the assistant actually gets things done, from checking a build to moving files around.
useWhen: Your work happens on Windows and the commands you need are PowerShell.
A command takes a long time and you want it to keep running in the background.
skipWhen: Your commands are written for bash and you do not want them rewritten.
You do not want the assistant running commands on your machine at all.
pros: Uses real Windows paths and environment variables, with no translating between dialects
Every command is tracked from the moment it starts, so you can watch long ones
A command that outlives its time limit keeps running and still reports its output
cons: Commands must be written in PowerShell; bash instructions are not converted.
Each command starts fresh, so folders and variables set earlier are gone.
Under the strictest safety boundary, some PowerShell features fail, such as Add-Type and COM objects.
Under that same boundary, a command that pipes output between programs also fails.

name: dsh-tool-pwsh-persistent
catalogDescription: Model-facing owner-scoped persistent PowerShell tool backed by the Harness PTY service
manifestDescription: Model-facing owner-scoped persistent PowerShell tool backed by the Harness PTY service

readme.description: The model-facing persistent pwsh tool for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging owner-scoped PowerShell state that survives across calls.
readme.summary: `dsh-tool-pwsh-persistent` gives each agent a `pwsh` tool that preserves its current directory, environment variables, functions, and background jobs across calls. Commands for one agent run sequentially, while different agents keep separate shell state. Choose it for multi-step PowerShell work; use `dsh-tool-pwsh` when every command should start clean, and use a terminal tool when commands require interactive stdin. Configure a pwsh-capable backend and per-command timeout; timeout or explicit `exit` discards the shell, so the next call starts fresh.

headings.text: What the agent can rely on

plain.headline: PowerShell that remembers
plain.oneLiner: One PowerShell window that keeps its state across commands.
plain.whatItDoes: Gives the assistant one PowerShell window that stays open between commands, so the folder it is in, the variables it set and the jobs it started are still there next time. Different assistants keep separate windows.
plain.whyYoudCare: Multi-step Windows work usually needs the previous step's settings, and this keeps them instead of starting over each time.
useWhen: A task needs several PowerShell commands that build on each other.
You set up an environment once and then keep working inside it.
skipWhen: You want every command to start from a clean, known state.
A command needs you to type input while it runs.
pros: Keeps folder, variables, functions and background jobs across commands
Commands from one assistant run in order, so they do not trip over each other
Each assistant gets its own shell state, so parallel work stays separate
cons: A time limit or an explicit exit throws the window away, so the next command starts fresh.
Typed input is echoed back into the output, and a long line can leave part of that echo behind.
Commands cannot wait for you to type input; such a command blocks until the time limit and resets the window.
On Windows, stop and hang-up signals are unavailable, so interrupting acts like pressing Ctrl-C in the console.

name: dsh-tool-ralph
catalogDescription: Model-facing fresh-agent Ralph loop over the workflow and subagent seams
manifestDescription: Model-facing fresh-agent Ralph loop over the workflow and subagent seams

readme.description: The model-facing ralph tool: a fixed foreground fresh-agent loop toward one immutable objective, for users and maintainers choosing or configuring fresh-agent iteration.
readme.summary: `ralph` runs a foreground sequence of fresh child agents against one immutable objective, with each round receiving only the previous bounded report and shared workspace state. It returns when a worker reports completion or a concrete blocker, or when the configured round limit is reached; those reports are not independently verified. Parent conversation and prior child sessions are never copied into a new round. Use it only when the direct human explicitly requests Ralph-style fresh-agent iteration; use goal tools for ordinary long-running work and subagents or workflows for bounded delegation.

rationale:
Fresh-agent Ralph iteration over a build-time-fixed script. Off by
default: the tool description restricts `ralph` to runs the human
explicitly asked for, and completion is a worker self-report, not an
independent evaluation. An overlay row restores it for a base-backed
profile (`$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml`, or a `--patch <file>`):
  - id: tool-ralph
    disabled: false

`base` ships this row disabled; the preset-plane gate reads declared row ids
without regard to `disabled`, so this row must stay to keep `tool-ralph` off
the host plane and out of collision with every preset's row.

plain.headline: Repeated fresh attempts
plain.oneLiner: Repeats a job with fresh helpers until one reports that it is done.
plain.whatItDoes: Runs the same job over and over, each time with a brand new helper that sees only a short report from the previous attempt plus the shared workspace. It stops when a helper says it is done, reports a real blocker, or hits the round limit.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is a way to grind through a stubborn task without dragging a long, tangled conversation along with it.
useWhen: You explicitly ask for a Ralph loop or repeated fresh-agent attempts.
A task is long and you accept that it may take many rounds.
skipWhen: You just want long-running work to continue; ordinary goal tracking fits better.
You need someone to confirm the work is truly finished before it stops.
pros: Each round starts clean, so earlier confusion does not pile up
It keeps going until the job is done or genuinely blocked, up to your round limit
Progress crosses rounds through the files in your shared workspace
cons: A helper decides on its own that the job is finished, and nothing independently checks that.
It runs in the foreground, so there is no job id to collect later and no checkpoint to resume from.
Only the workspace carries information forward; a helper's reasoning is thrown away.
If one round fails, the whole run stops there and is not retried.
Only the number of rounds limits the effort, not a token, cost or time budget.

name: dsh-tool-skill
catalogDescription: Model-facing skill loading tool for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Model-facing skill loading tool for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: The model-facing skill catalog and loader tool for users and maintainers understanding what agents see, or configuring the session skill catalog.
readme.summary: Agents can discover and load skills during a session. Before the first request, when model-invocable skills exist and the `skill` tool is visible, they receive a durable catalog of available skill names and capped descriptions, and can use the `skill` tool to load full instructions. Users can invoke a user-invocable skill with `/name`, which injects the same instructions into that step. Catalog changes append a complete replacement, including an empty catalog that retires old names; configure `catalogDescriptionMaxLength` to limit each description.

plain.headline: Load skills on demand
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant find and load your written skill instructions.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets the assistant see which skills exist and pull one in when it is relevant. You can also type a skill name after a slash to apply that skill to the next step.
plain.whyYoudCare: Skills carry your house rules for a kind of task, and this is how the assistant finds and follows them.
useWhen: You keep written instructions for recurring tasks and want them followed.
You want to start a step with a specific skill by typing its name.
skipWhen: You have no skills written and do not plan to add any.
Skill loading is already handled some other way.
pros: The assistant can find the right skill mid-task instead of you pasting instructions
A short list of names sits in front of the assistant, so it knows what is available
You can apply a skill yourself by typing its name after a slash
cons: The list shows only names and shortened descriptions, so the choice rests on those.
A loaded skill has no size limit and can eat a large part of the next step's room.
A skill may point at files, but nothing fetches or attaches them for you.
One change to the list re-sends the whole list, which costs room in the conversation.

name: dsh-tool-str-replace-editor
catalogDescription: Model-facing view, create, literal replace, and line insert tool over the Harness filesystem service
manifestDescription: Model-facing view, create, literal replace, and line insert tool over the Harness filesystem service

readme.description: The standalone str_replace_editor tool over ctx.fs for users and maintainers composing Claude-Code-style file editing for agents.
readme.summary: `dsh-tool-str-replace-editor` provides a standalone model-facing `str_replace_editor` tool over `ctx.fs`: `view` shows numbered file content or a shallow directory listing, `create` makes a new file, `str_replace` applies a unique literal replacement, and `insert` adds lines at a chosen boundary. It is composable with persistent Bash, one-shot Bash, sandboxed Bash, or another terminal surface. Mutations obey the same read-before-edit policy and sandbox fence as the rest of the fs family, enforced by whichever backend and policy plugins are mounted. Choose it when a deployment wants the Claude-Code-style single editor tool with absolute paths; the `dsh-tool-fs` package provides the alternative `read`/`write`/`edit` suite.

plain.headline: One tool to view and edit files
plain.oneLiner: A single tool for viewing, creating and editing text files.

useWhen: You are assembling a setup that expects this specific editing tool.
Your files are plain text and you want exact-match edits.
skipWhen: You use the built-in file tools; they already cover reading, writing and editing.
You work with images, archives or other non-text files.
pros: One tool covers viewing, creating, exact replacements and line inserts
It refuses the edit unless the text you named appears exactly once, so the wrong spot is not changed
It works with whichever file storage is already set up
cons: Only plain text files; images and other binary files are unsupported.
It will not replace every occurrence of a phrase; zero matches or several matches are refused.
Without the safety and file checks in place, edits go through with no checks at all.

name: dsh-tool-subagent

readme.description: Model-facing subagent delegation tool for users and maintainers configuring, composing, or debugging delegation over a subagent provider.
readme.summary: Use this package to give an agent a named tool that delegates work to a configured child-agent backend. In `one-shot` mode, calls wait for the child by default; in `continuable` mode, they start a persistent child in the background and return an id for later messages. Supported backends can also expose approved child LLM providers, models, and reasoning effort for selection. Each instance can set child persona, tool access, and depth limits, while failed runs return errors instead of partial success.

rationale:
Fork omits model selection so provider/model stay equal to the parent and
the inherited history remains eligible for KV Cache reuse. This base row
stays one-shot; preset layers may select continuable mode without adding a
child-only system-prompt section or tool schema ahead of that history.
See .agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-08-18-model-selected-subagent-routes.md
and .agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-08-10-fork-children-stay-one-shot.md.

Host-owned opt-in sampled when a new Web session receives its preset
delegation tools. The Plugins page edits this settings namespace.

plain.headline: Hand work to helper agents
plain.oneLiner: Lets the assistant delegate work to separate helper agents.
plain.whatItDoes: Lets the assistant pass a piece of work to a separate helper agent, either waiting for the result or starting the helper in the background and messaging it later. Each helper can have its own persona, tools and depth.
plain.whyYoudCare: Large jobs get split up, and your main conversation does not fill with every side detail.
useWhen: A task splits into independent pieces that can run at the same time.
You want a focused helper with a narrower set of tools.
skipWhen: The work is small enough to do directly in one conversation.
You need the helper's result handed back as the answer to the call.
pros: Separate helpers keep their own context, so the main conversation stays readable
Helpers can run in the background while other work continues
You can pick a different AI service, model or reasoning effort for a helper when the setup allows it
Failed runs report an error instead of pretending to be a partial success
cons: A background helper's result is not returned here; you read it in that helper's own session.
Several helpers sharing one tool name are only caught late, which can waste a start.
The helper that copies your conversation cannot pick another AI service, because the shared history has to stay reusable.
Changing a helper's persona, tools or depth needs a second, separately named tool.

name: dsh-tool-subagent-control

readme.description: Global send_message, interrupt_agent, and list_agents tools for users and maintainers composing or debugging continuable-child control.
readme.summary: `dsh-tool-subagent-control` adds the global control tools for continuable children: `send_message` steers between a direct parent and child, `interrupt_agent` stops a child's current turn while keeping its inbox and descendants intact, and `list_agents` (from the separately loadable `list-agents` plugin) lists continuable children by durable id and label. Parents and continuable children inherit the same `send_message` definition and ordering, so model communication adds no child-only tool schema. No tool's presence decides whether a delegation tool starts continuable work.

rationale:
Continuable background children are selected per delegation tool. The
separately loaded follow-up tool registers the one global `send_message`.

The subagent registry and its backends STAY in the host plane. `subagents` is
a process singleton with a cross-session query surface (`listChildren`,
`followup`) that the host api-proxy serves to the browser, and a provider
registers under a globally unique name, so a per-session copy would both
starve that host row and collide on the second session. What a preset
chooses is which delegation TOOLS its agent sees, below.

plain.headline: Message and stop helpers
plain.oneLiner: Tools for messaging, stopping and listing background helper agents.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds tools for the assistant to send a follow-up message to a helper agent it started, stop that helper's current turn without throwing away what is waiting for it, and list the helpers it has.
plain.whyYoudCare: Once helpers run in the background you need a way to steer one or call it off before it finishes.
useWhen: You run background helper agents that may need correcting while they work.
You want to stop one helper without losing the others.
skipWhen: Your helpers always run start to finish and never need guidance.
You are not using background helper agents at all.
pros: You can correct a helper's direction without starting it over
Stopping a helper keeps its waiting messages and its own helpers intact
Parents and helpers share one messaging tool, so no extra instructions are needed
cons: A delivered message has no result of its own; any reply is a separate message.
Only neighbouring agents can talk: siblings and deeper helpers cannot message each other.
The helper list is a snapshot and can be out of date the moment you read it.
There is no paging and no way to remove a helper from the list.

You want the plan to still be there when you come back later.
skipWhen: The task is a single step or a quick question.
Several assistants need to share one list.

It survives turns and reopened sessions, so nothing is lost
It can allow more than one task in progress for work that runs in parallel
cons: Only the one assistant session that owns it can change it.

readme.summary: Use `dsh-web` to search the web or fetch a URL without tying callers to a specific vendor. It selects a usable backend for each operation and gives callers consistent cancellation, errors, and result limits. Choose it for plugins or tools that call `ctx.web.search()` or `ctx.web.fetch()`; the shipped `dsh-tool-web` tools load it for you. A search or fetch requires a configured, usable provider because this package does not make network requests on its own.

rationale:
The shared base enables the stable model-facing web_search and web_fetch
tools. The Web app disables this host row and composes both tools per agent
preset; products with a stricter network policy override tool-web. DeepSeek
search resolves the same DEEPSEEK_API_KEY
credential the Models page manages for chat, at each search; its Messages
endpoint is configured independently from the model route, so it takes its own
base-URL override. Anonymous fetch accepts only public HTTP(S) destinations,
resolves and validates every destination, and pins every actual connection.
Search is a full auxiliary model request with server-side retrieval, so this
shipped DeepSeek route gets 60s while the provider-neutral tool default
remains 30s.

plain.headline: One doorway for web search and page reads
plain.oneLiner: The shared doorway that search and page-reading tools go through.
plain.whatItDoes: A shared doorway that lets the assistant search the web or open a page without depending on one particular company's service. It picks a working backend for each request and returns consistent errors and size limits.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the part that keeps web access working even when the service behind it changes.
useWhen: A tool needs to search or read pages and you want to avoid tying it to one company.
You want to pin one particular search or page-reading service.
skipWhen: Your setup never reaches the web, in which case this doorway does nothing.
You are happy with the shipped search and page-reading tools as they are.
pros: You can swap the search or page-reading service without changing the tools
Calls share consistent cancellation, error codes, and result limits
The shipped search and page-reading tools pull it in for you
cons: It needs at least one working service behind it; with none, every call fails
There is no way to check whether a service is available short of trying it
Search carries a query and a result count only; date, domain, and region controls are still to come
It cannot read PDFs, and page extraction by a service is out of scope for now

name: dsh-web-app
catalogDescription: The dsh browser-surface bundle: the web patch layer over dsh-base plus the runtime glue plugin (frontend dist serving, web-surface prompt, bash runtime variables, URL line)
manifestDescription: The dsh browser-surface bundle: the web patch layer over dsh-base plus the runtime glue plugin (frontend dist serving, web-surface prompt, bash runtime variables, URL line)

readme.description: The browser GUI for dsh: interactive chat, model and settings management, and session history, for users running the dsh web surface.
readme.summary: Run `dsh --profile web` to open an interactive browser GUI with chat, model and settings management, and session history. It uses the same model access, tools, and safety defaults as other dsh surfaces. Startup prints an authenticated URL and normally opens it in the default browser; SSH sessions and `--no-open` leave the URL for manual opening. You can change the port and allow extra hosts, but cannot bind all network interfaces. Choose this package for interactive browser work; use `dsh-headless` for one-shot command-line tasks.

rationale:
Ordinary provider for the parsed Web flags. Its plugin-level injection
waits for cmdlineArgs; no launcher metadata or special row kind is needed.

Web glue owned by this bundle: resolves the built frontend dist (an
assembly fact of dsh-web-app, never user config), mounts the
frontend-static fallback owner, registers the web-surface prompt
section and the bash runtime variable, prints the URL line, and opens the
canonical local URL after the full Loader tree settles and the required-
entry audit passes. The
webStartup provider supplies invocation-only values; after the server binds, this row samples
LAN trust once and provides `webRuntime`. A complete agent-preset persona
suppresses the prompt section for that agent while retaining the host-owned
shell variable.

plain.headline: Open the assistant in your browser
plain.oneLiner: The browser window where you chat with the assistant.
plain.whatItDoes: Starts an interactive browser window for the assistant, with chat, model and settings management, and your session history. It uses the same models, tools, and safety defaults as the other ways of running the harness.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is the comfortable way to work: a real window with history and settings instead of a command line.
useWhen: You want to chat with the assistant in a browser window.
You want to manage models, settings, and past sessions in one place.
skipWhen: You are running one-shot command-line tasks; a different package covers those.
You cannot build the browser files from a source checkout yet.
pros: Startup prints a link and usually opens it for you
You can change the port and allow extra host names
It keeps the same models, tools, and safety defaults as the other ways of running the harness
cons: From a source checkout you must build the browser files first, with no fallback
Binding all network interfaces is refused for safety, so it stays on the loopback address
It reports only that the browser was asked to open, not that it actually did
In a remote session you get the link but must open it yourself through your client
Only a setting inherited from your environment can choose which browser opens

name: dsh-web-fetch-http
catalogDescription: Anonymous public HTTP(S) fetch provider for the DeepSeek Harness web capability seam (ctx.web)
manifestDescription: Anonymous public HTTP(S) fetch provider for the DeepSeek Harness web capability seam (ctx.web)

readme.description: The anonymous public HTTP(S) fetch backend for ctx.web: how deployments mount bounded, safe URL retrieval with same-origin redirects and text-only decoding.
readme.summary: With `dsh-web-fetch-http`, the harness can fetch public HTTP(S) pages through the web service (`ctx.web`) and get their status code plus bounded, decoded content without sending credentials. Choose it when a composition needs safe retrieval with URL validation, public-address resolution, connection pinning, same-origin redirects, byte and character caps, and an explicit product `User-Agent`. It returns non-2xx responses as results rather than errors, and rejects non-public destinations, binary data, and unsupported content types. The model-facing `web_fetch` tool lives in `dsh-tool-web`, which renders this provider's bodies.

plain.headline: Read a public web page safely
plain.oneLiner: Fetches public web pages with safety checks and output limits.
plain.whatItDoes: Fetches public web pages for the assistant without sending any credentials. It validates the address, refuses anything that is not publicly reachable, and caps how much text comes back.
plain.whyYoudCare: It lets the assistant read a page you point at while keeping the request safe and bounded.
useWhen: You paste a link and want the assistant to read that page.
You want page reads that send no credentials and stay inside size limits.
skipWhen: The page needs a login or sits on a private network.
The content is a PDF or another non-text format.
pros: No credentials are ever sent with the request
Every resolved address must be public, and each connection is pinned to it
Redirects cannot escape the site you started from
Replies are capped in size, and a non-success code comes back as a result rather than an error
cons: Only text-based pages decode, so a missing or binary content type is refused
The character set is read from the response header alone, ignoring any page-level declaration
Reading text out of PDFs is not supported yet

name: dsh-web-search-deepseek
catalogDescription: DeepSeek-backed search provider (native web_search via the Anthropic-compatible API) for the DeepSeek Harness web capability seam (ctx.web)
manifestDescription: DeepSeek-backed search provider (native web_search via the Anthropic-compatible API) for the DeepSeek Harness web capability seam (ctx.web)

readme.description: The DeepSeek-backed search provider for ctx.web: how deployments mount native DeepSeek web search through the Anthropic-compatible Messages API, with per-search credential resolution.
readme.summary: With `dsh-web-search-deepseek`, the harness searches the web through DeepSeek's native search using the DeepSeek account sign-in or an existing `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`. Choose it when a deployment wants DeepSeek native search and accepts that one search costs a full model turn in latency and tokens, because DeepSeek exposes no dedicated search endpoint. Results come from the structured search blocks DeepSeek returns, never from scraping text out of a reply. A missing credential fails the call with a structured error; a response without a search-result block fails loudly rather than degrading. The model-facing `web_search` tool lives in `dsh-tool-web`.

plain.headline: Web search through your DeepSeek account
plain.oneLiner: Searches the web through DeepSeek using your existing account.
plain.whatItDoes: Answers a search by asking DeepSeek to run it on its servers, using the account you already signed in with or an existing key. Results come from the structured search data DeepSeek returns, never from text scraped out of a written reply.
plain.whyYoudCare: You get current answers from the web without signing up for a separate search service.
useWhen: You signed in with a DeepSeek account or already hold a key.
You want search results taken from structured data rather than a written reply.
skipWhen: The cost or the waiting time of each search matters more than the convenience.
You have no DeepSeek credential available at all.
pros: No separate search subscription is needed
Results come from structured search data, not text scraped out of a reply
A missing credential fails with a clear error instead of a vague answer
cons: Every search runs as a full model turn, so it costs time and generated words
A reply that contains no search result fails loudly rather than degrading quietly
Only the sources actually cited in the reply come with a snippet
The number of results is trimmed afterwards, because the service offers no count control

name: dsh-webhook
catalogDescription: Fire-and-forget webhook rule runtime that creates Workspace-backed DeepSeek Harness Sessions
manifestDescription: Fire-and-forget webhook rule runtime that creates Workspace-backed DeepSeek Harness Sessions

readme.description: Webhook rule runtime for maintainers registering trusted external-event policies that create Workspace Sessions.
readme.summary: `dsh-webhook` provides the Host `ctx.webhookRuntime`: a registry for trusted programmatic webhook rules plus the one built-in action, creating an ordinary root Session inside a Web Workspace. The interface stays at `register(rule)` and `dispatch(delivery)`; provider authentication belongs to adapter packages. Use it when a trusted rule must turn an external event into a new agent Session.

plain.headline: Turn outside events into new sessions
plain.oneLiner: Internal plumbing that turns outside events into new assistant sessions.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that lets trusted rules turn an event sent by another service into a brand-new assistant session in a workspace folder. It has no settings of its own.
plain.whyYoudCare: Only worth your attention if you are wiring an outside service to start assistant sessions automatically.
useWhen: You are building an automation that should start a new assistant session when something happens elsewhere.
You need incoming events to be handled by your own trusted code.
skipWhen: You just want to use the assistant in this app, where this is not fitted.
pros: Lets an outside event start a fresh session in a folder you choose.
Sign-in details for each service live in separate add-on packs, not here.
Rules are registered and called through one simple pair of actions.
cons: Calls are fire-and-forget: if the program crashes, events that had not started a session are lost, with no queue or retry.
Nothing stops the same event arriving twice, so repeated messages can create repeated sessions.
Accepting an event says nothing about whether the assistant succeeded or produced anything.
Shutting it down asks its callbacks to stop but cannot force unrelated code in the same program to end.
A failed attempt can leave an empty workspace folder behind.

name: dsh-webhook-github
catalogDescription: Signed GitHub HTTP webhook adapter for the DeepSeek Harness webhook runtime
manifestDescription: Signed GitHub HTTP webhook adapter for the DeepSeek Harness webhook runtime

readme.description: Signed GitHub webhook adapter for deployments routing authenticated JSON events into the webhook runtime.
readme.summary: `dsh-webhook-github` registers one exact HTTP route on the injected `ctx.webServer`. It bounds and verifies GitHub's raw JSON body, projects a provider-neutral delivery, calls `ctx.webhookRuntime.dispatch()`, and returns `202` without waiting for rules or Sessions. Use it when a deployment needs authenticated GitHub ingress for the generic webhook runtime.

plain.headline: Accept signed messages from GitHub
plain.oneLiner: Receives signed GitHub event messages and hands them to your rules.
plain.whatItDoes: Adds one web address that accepts GitHub's automatic event messages, checks the secret they are signed with, and passes them to your webhook rules. It answers straight away without waiting for the work.
plain.whyYoudCare: You would only set this up if GitHub needs to trigger assistant work for you automatically.
useWhen: You want a GitHub event, such as a new issue, to start work in the harness.
Your GitHub messages must be checked as genuinely sent by GitHub.
skipWhen: Your setup does not use GitHub, or you are not running a web address for it.
pros: Confirms messages really came from GitHub before anything acts on them.
Limits how large a message may be before it is refused.
Answers GitHub immediately, so GitHub is not left waiting for the work.
cons: It has no secure connection of its own and belongs behind a secure proxy or tunnel.
It checks only the message shape, so your rules must check the GitHub details they use.
The immediate reply does not tell GitHub whether any work was actually done.
GitHub must send JSON; a form-encoded message is refused.
You must supply a source name, an address path, a secret reference and a size limit.

name: dsh-win32-process
catalogDescription: Shared low-level Win32 process, stdio, and Job Object primitives
manifestDescription: Shared low-level Win32 process, stdio, and Job Object primitives

readme.description: Low-level Win32 process primitives for maintainers implementing or debugging the Windows ACL sandbox and ordinary subprocess Job runner.
readme.summary: This low-level Win32 process library is consumed by the Windows ACL sandbox and the ordinary subprocess Job runner. It owns the repository's one Koffi binding table for reusable process, stdio, and Job Object operations; it is not a Cordis service and does not choose sandbox policy or public child behavior. Read this page when maintaining either native process path or checking its handle-lifetime limits.

plain.headline: Low-level Windows process calls
plain.oneLiner: Internal Windows-only helpers for starting and stopping programs. Nothing to configure.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block for the low-level Windows calls that start programs, carry their input and output, and group them so they can be stopped together. It runs only on Windows, inside safety and process code.

name: dsh-workflow
catalogDescription: Workflow capability seam: ctx.workflowEngine service, run vocabulary, and workflow/* events
manifestDescription: Workflow capability seam: ctx.workflowEngine service, run vocabulary, and workflow/* events

readme.description: The workflow orchestration capability: run a model-written script that fans out subagents, for users and maintainers choosing or building on ctx.workflowEngine.
readme.summary: Run a plain-JavaScript orchestration script that fans work out to subagents and returns the script's final JSON value. Scripts can use `agent()`, `parallel()`, `pipeline()`, `phase()`, and `log()`; models normally access them through the `workflow` tool. Each run belongs to its caller, attributes every child to the invoking agent, resolves failures and cancellation without rejecting its result, and awaits script and child cleanup during disposal. The caller must supply an execution engine, allowing the isolation strategy to change without altering visible behavior.

plain.headline: Spreads work across helper agents
plain.oneLiner: Internal engine that runs scripts coordinating helper agents. Nothing to configure.
plain.whatItDoes: An internal building block that runs a short script which spreads work across many helper agents and gathers the result. Models reach it through the workflow tool, so there is nothing for you to configure.

name: dsh-workflow-ptc
catalogDescription: Workflow orchestration in the shared sandboxed Node PTC runtime
manifestDescription: Workflow orchestration in the shared sandboxed Node PTC runtime

readme.description: Run workflow orchestration through the shared sandboxed PTC Node process runtime, with workflow hooks, subagent routing and caller-owned cancellation.
readme.summary: Run JavaScript workflows in fresh Node processes under the calling Session's file sandbox policy. Scripts keep the `agent()`, `parallel()`, `pipeline()`, `phase()` and `log()` hooks while subagents perform delegated work. The same execution provider serves PTC and workflows, including the opt-in Ralph loop. Runs have no overall elapsed deadline; cancellation stops the managed process and disposes child agents. The selected sandbox and subprocess providers determine enforcement and cleanup limits.

plain.headline: Run scripted jobs across many helpers
plain.oneLiner: Runs scripted jobs that spread work across many helper assistants.
plain.whatItDoes: Runs a script that hands parts of a job to several helper assistants at once, each in a fresh process under your session's file safety limits. It keeps simple helpers for starting agents, running them side by side, chaining steps and reporting progress.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is how one request can be split across many helper assistants without you writing the coordination yourself.
useWhen: A job has many independent pieces you want done at the same time.
You want a repeatable script instead of driving each helper by hand.
skipWhen: You are happy with one assistant working through a task step by step.
Your setup uses the Python execution path, which must leave this switched off.
pros: Several helper assistants can work at the same time on separate pieces.
Scripts get ready-made helpers for side-by-side work, chained stages and progress notes.
Scripts run inside the same file safety limits as your session.
Cancelling a run stops the process and clears up the helper assistants it started.
cons: File limits and cleanup depend on the parts you plug in, not on this engine alone.
The caps on how much work a script may do are cooperative, not enforced security limits.
A run has no overall time limit; it stays active until it finishes, fails or is cancelled.
The restricted script environment is not a security boundary; system rules govern code that reaches the runtime underneath.
Errors crossing that boundary do not match the usual error check, so scripts should test error names and codes.

name: dsh-workspace
catalogDescription: Workspace entity registry (ctx.workspaceRegistry): durable workspace records with validated session attachment over the domain data form for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Workspace entity registry (ctx.workspaceRegistry): durable workspace records with validated session attachment over the domain data form for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: Workspace entity registry (ctx.workspaceRegistry) for hosts choosing, mounting, or debugging durable workspace records and header-validated session membership.
readme.summary: Use this package to keep an ordered, persistent list of project directories and the sessions run in each directory. Hosts can build project sidebars, hide sessions from grouping without deleting their histories, and remove projects without deleting folders, files, or sessions. Re-adding a removed directory creates a fresh project, while sessions whose directories cannot be validated remain ungrouped. Choose it for GUI or host workflows that need durable project grouping; it is invisible to models and adds no prompt or request-context cost, but requires session persistence and storage backends.

headings.text: Hiding and restoring sessions, and removing projects

plain.headline: Keep your project folders in a list
plain.oneLiner: Remembers your projects and groups sessions by folder.
plain.whatItDoes: Keeps an ordered, lasting list of the project folders you use and the sessions run in each one, so the app can show a project list and group sessions by folder. The model never sees it and it adds nothing to your requests.
plain.whyYoudCare: It is what lets the app remember your projects and group sessions by folder between visits.
useWhen: You want the app to show a project list and group sessions by folder.
You want to hide a project from grouping without deleting anything.
skipWhen: You only ever work in one folder and never use a project list.
pros: Projects keep their order and survive restarts.
Hiding a session from a project leaves its history untouched.
Removing a project leaves your folders, files and sessions in place.
It costs nothing in your requests because the model never sees it.
cons: Removing a project never deletes anything; those sessions just stop being grouped.
A session joins a project only when its record holds a folder path that still matches.
If another program deletes or damages a folder, the app notices only at the next refresh or restart.
Archiving and restoring apply different checks, so restoring an entry whose session is gone still succeeds.
A turn that starts just as you archive a session can stay visible while it runs, in practice for one step.

name: dsh-workspace-changes
catalogDescription: Per-turn workspace file changes recorded from git working-tree snapshots and whole-file captures, with per-file comparisons, for the DeepSeek Harness
manifestDescription: Per-turn workspace file changes recorded from git working-tree snapshots and whole-file captures, with per-file comparisons, for the DeepSeek Harness

readme.description: Summarize each top-level turn's changed files from git working-tree snapshots and whole-file captures around file-tool edits, announce them with a workspace/changes Session event, and serve the summary and per-file comparisons while the Session lives; configuration, repository requirement, and coverage rules.
readme.summary: This plugin summarizes which files each top-level turn changed, with per-file line counts, and serves each listed file's turn-start and turn-end comparison. Git snapshots of the working tree at turn start and turn end are diffed; every file a file tool edits is copied whole before its first edit and again at turn end, covering the files git does not. Without a repository or git, only file-tool edits are listed. The Session log receives one `workspace/changes` event naming the turn; summaries and comparisons stay on the Host until the Session is disposed. The Web changed-files card renders them.

rationale:
Records each top-level turn's changed files from git working-tree
snapshots; the changed-files card above renders its events.

plain.headline: See which files each turn changed
plain.oneLiner: Shows which files each turn changed, with per-file comparisons.
plain.whatItDoes: Records which files each of your turns changed and shows a card listing them, with line counts per file and a before-and-after view. It compares git snapshots from the start and end of the turn and keeps its own copies of files edited by file tools.
plain.whyYoudCare: It gives you a quick record of what the assistant actually touched in each turn.
useWhen: You want to check what changed before you accept a turn's work.
You want per-file before-and-after views without running git yourself.
skipWhen: You already track changes yourself, or you need the record to outlive a restart.
pros: Shows the files each turn changed, with line counts per file.
Gives a before-and-after view of each listed file.
Covers files git ignores by keeping its own copy around file-tool edits.
Still lists file-tool edits when the folder is not a git repository.
cons: The record lives only as long as the session; after a restart, earlier turns have no card or comparison.
It needs git 2.13 or later, and a git problem abandons the turn's record with a warning.
The first snapshot of a session copies every untracked, non-ignored file, which can use a lot of temporary space.
Edits you make during a turn are counted as part of that turn.
In a folder outside git, only files a file tool names are captured, so shell edits are missing.
